FLOUR IT IS THE BEST. The Examiner, Saturday, April 7,1906.

sometfung to (to with the cleiay ; anyway it was the longest of all the dreary days which ' Lord Alanale had spent in prison, and it seemed to him it would never end, On Monday morning he heard the sound of the Alaudale bells ringing out a merry peal, their music floating on the breeze across the miles which S epar at ed him from his home. The bells cheered poor Kenneth strangely; they seemed a taste of home. He wondered who was married; surely someone of conse- quencp for the bells' to peal, and yet the grander weddings were generally later in the day. The door was flung open wide to admit Captain Grimlay ' and two important looking strangers, the two last having coma from Lon- don bringing with them the necessary order for Lord Ala.ndale's rzinse. ,
But Joe Fielding whs not there. Sir John Leigh, staunch friend and comrade, was :absent too—what did it mean? A strange sense of loneliness and desertion seized on Kenneth.

" I think someone might have cone to drive hOme with me," he said in a disappointed tone. ' "Lady Mary and. Miss Jardine are waiting for you at Woodlands said Captain Grimla.y. " You will find Mr. Fielding and other friends there too. You see," he added with a happy inspiration, "I suppose thtP-r, felt you could hardly make room ibr them all here and would not take adVantagc of each other. You will find the yillage-'en.fete, and the bells are ring- jug joyously in your honour." ' That cheery peal was for him then, not for some happy brad pair. The thought set Lord Alandale wondering how soon these bells would chime again—for him and Helen. The Aland& carriage was waiting, sent for him by Lady Lady Mary's orders ; it was the state landau drawn by a pair of dashing greys, and it looked not 'unlike a bridal chariot 1 it was strange Lord Alandale felt in the dark after- time how oddly and persistently- his mind ran on weddings this morning.

The drive in the open air did him good after those weeks of clo:.z confinement. However much people had doubted, him once, they seemed convinced Of their error now and only too anxious to atone for past suspicions, for spectators thronged the village lanes, women called blessings ,on his head, and children flung little posies of wild flowers into the car- riage. _

Woodlands at last ! Quite a crowd in the hall to greet him. Lady Mary in the forefront with Magdalen beside her. Sir John Leigh,, Joe Fielding, the Rector, and—could it be possi- ble—Mr. Mackenzie and his daughter in the rear, but the face Alandale longed for, the face whose image was printed on his heart,' wav absent. Wbare. oh 1 where was Helen

Sir John simply, ana tnen Joe rielcung• 'took up the story. • You must not think us heartless enough not to try to find Miss Jardine. As soon as it was ascertained she went to London, I set . a detective on her track, but he could find out nothing, • absolutely nothing; except ' that - shit did not take a cab at King's Cross; .she waited some time at the station and then 14ft it on foot. "His theory was that. she had friends in the suburbs and went out to them by one of the early workmen's trams, but he could find no clue ; he wished to advertise, offering a reward for information, but such a course must cause i publicity which I thought you would wish to avoid." " I will take the search into my' own hands," said Alandale, " and love will find the way.",a,o • Sir John hesitated. "I hate telling you, but your cousin; Mag- dalen, has' the strangest theory about Miss Helen's disappearance. You are sure to hear it ,at Alandale Hall; but as both Lady Mary and her niece feel rather strongly on the subject their version will possibly., be an exaggerated one, Will you Wait to hear it or shall Field- •' ing tell you a plain unvarnished tale '? " " I would much rather hear the story from you," said Alandale. "Lady Mary Was always jealous of Helen on Magdalen's ac- count, and Magdalen can hardly be fair to the girl Whose very existence robs her of a for- tune." "I think Myself that Magdalen is incapable , g jealousy or malice," said Sir John, "but I will leave Fielding to .tell the story." "On the • afternoon of that fatal Wednes- day," began the lawyer, ".a foreign letter reached the Hall addressed to Miss Hildred Jasper, • care of Lady Mary Jardine.' Lady_ Mary told the butler to give it to Miss Jardine. and it was put 'into her hands as she started with me for Leigh Court, but I noticed that she slipped it into her pocket unread: .! "Later on. when it became certain Miss Jardine had disappeared, Lady Mary remem- bered that letter, and it came back to her that Miss Jardine had declared over and over again that her companion Hildred Jasper was abso- lutely alone in the world. When asked to send the news of the; poor ,girl's death to , her ',people,' she had asserted fhat there was no living creature -who would care what, became of Hildred. You will remember the certifi cate of rnarriagoefound among Norton's papers clearly proving that he had been .inarried under an asSumedname to Hildred Jasper." "I don't se what that has to do with Helen." Well, it is the foundation on which Lady Mary bases her theory. . She believes the girl we knew as the heiress of Alandale is really Hildred Jasper and that the'tru,e Helen Jar- dine avas drowned." " It's simply . impossible," said „Lord Alan- dale ; " I will never bdlieve it, never." Sir John hesitated. • There ;are ,some grounds for it, Alandale. It explains why your supposed cousin met Norton by night, it eXplainsawhy she 'gave him (as she undoubtedly did) all th.;" money' at her disposal, • but it leaves two problems unsolved: how is it that none of the survivors •of the Cygnet's ' crew and passengers exposed- the fraud', and how in that. 'case. should poor Gresham have taken her for his fiancee ? " Fielding interposed. "The strongest • argument i favour of. Lady Mary's story is this : Granted that Helen Jar- dine left Leigh Court intending to return to Alandale, what changed her !Matti and, made her .go to London ? She 'was absolutely alone in the fly, so no outside • influence could have been brought- ,to bear on her. Well, Lady Mary says she suddenly. remembered the letter addressed to Hildred Jasper 'and opening it discovered that some associate of her former life was on her track and was 'coining here to • denounce her." • " I don't believe it," said- Lord Alendale positively ; " you haven't shaken my trust ie Helen yet." Neither did the accusations of Lady Mary, a_ca were reluctantly endorsed by Milealtiim. The Earl only told- the two ladies they were unfair to Helen and judged, her falsely. Then Lady Mary played her trump card. "If a second letter comes addressed to 'Hildred Jasper,' I shall take Upon myself td open it ; we must at least know the truth. You seem to forget that, if my theory is right. Magdalen has been robbed, of home and for- tune by a Shameful imposter," " So be it," said Lord Alandale ; such a letter comes, open it by all means '; I feel 'that it will clear my Helen from even thd suspicion of fraud." . But Lord Alandale did not have, to wait for the arrival of a 'second letter addressed to " Hildred Jasper" at tile Hall. The next morning, as he Unlocked his poet bag at Woodlands, among the dozena of con- gratulatory notes felicitating him on the clearing of his name and restoration of fdA liberty he found a plain unpretentiouS-losik;ng white envelope with a penny -stamp embossed in the corner. The laimlwriting 'sent pulses jumping with eager anxiety ; he swept the other missives aside and locking the dome against all intruders opened the letter ht` guessed was from, his- life's love. There was no date, no heading, the few Lines had evidently been written in paned in haste.. • "My darling,—You must forget that you ever loved me and think of Me no more. I have robbed the dead and -the hying, bat I -won't let you discover the truth from othees you shall hear it from. me. I was' ,Iiil; keel 'Jasper, and am now 'Eldred Blake; vi;icjw :of the man murdered in the , Aland grounds. I married him when I was almost a child and his evil deeds am.; cruelty well nigh be my heart— A garsire:.! Samaritan paid for my musical trainii:-.g my husband was serving time at Poetise i and I went out to St. Moaica's Colleae, bourne, as teacher of 'music and singing: " There I met your cousin, and what She was to me I cannot tell you ; I think her love saved me from despair ; her affection for ra.? and mine for her was like that of Dey;fl anti Jonathan, " passing the love of woman.' " She wanted me to return to England Wi her as her companion and I agreed, :or coabi not face the loneliness of life hi Melboarea without her. I swear to. you • that .I . had no thought of fraud when we left •Melbourne but I was a wretched sailor, Helen a good one; we had been three days at sea before I was able to leave my cabin, and, in those three days my friend had made herself a general favourite with officers. and passengers. The‘first time I could go on deck Helen told me that everyone had (she looked so young and girlish) taken her for the companion and me for, the heiress. She had let the mistake' go unchallenged and so I found our identitieS reversed. • • " What ! could I do ? She; begged awl prayed me to let the comedy go on, fore': e had broken off her engagement with Charles Gresham before leaving Australia and there was someone on board she was beginning to love ; he was rather a stern, ultra honoureble man; and she thought he would torn against her if he found she had deceived him. • ".For her sake J let the farce go on, 'and when the fire broke out Helen and her lover left the ship in one of the boats, having, as I thought, a far better chance of life than I had,

div.head: • CHAPTER XXVIJ
div.p: • CHAPTER XXVIJ

"'WnnitE is Helen? Why is she not nee to greet me ? " Lord Alandale spoke curtly, angrily, and his ;dbating aunt (cousin in point of blood, but he had always regarded her as the nearer relation) looked frightened at the cloud on his face. Was it for this that she and Magdalen had counted the hours till he should • be restored to them ? Was ,it for this that they had yearned for his return ? They had loved him for years and neither of ; the twd had ever caused him 'a moment's pain, yet they were as nothing to him compared with the girl " from over the sea " whom he had .known only a few short months and who had—it seemed to Magdalen and Lady Mary -,brought with herea sheaf of sorrow. Once, twice the elder lady tried to speak and answer Lord Alandale's imperious de- mand, but each time she broke Own' horr- lessly, and in the end' it was Magdalen \vim . took the reply upon herself. "We have not seen Helen since Wednesday evening. Sir John put her in a fly then at ; half-past seven and told the man to drive her to Alandale Hall. The Hyman declares she stopped him at the cross roads and ordered him to take her to Thornby Station. Mr. Fielding made enquiries there and found rnat she certainly went up to London by the night mail, but we have learned nothing more. 'Sir John Leigh interposed. I was the last person—except the flyman —to speak to Miss Jardine and I will give you all the information in my power presently ; meanwhile I want to iatroduc,e you to the heroine to whom you owe your freedom. ;But for Miss Mackenzie's brave determined search for the revolver which killed poor Norton, I fear we should never have got ori the track of the ;real murderer ; Miss Mackenzie, allow me to present to von my .o.lct friend, 'Lord Alan- 'dale, who owes his life and honour 'to your courage." Fenn_th was no churl, but a gentleman of long descent; his very heart ached for news of Helen, but he did not attempt to shitk the duty evidently expected of him ; bowing low over Maria Mackenzie 's, hand he raised it . gallantly to his lips. " I thank you with all my/heart," he sait simply. " Mr. Mackenzie." and he turned the ironmaster, " I shah, neVer forget youi daughter's goodness." " I reckon," said Peter rathgr sheepishly " I done a bit myself to blacken things against n you, so Maria's only made the balace. even If you'll be content to let bygones be bygones, my lord, I should be grateful." Lord Alandale shook the proffered hand, a servant appeared with champagne, and all those_ present drank the Earl's . health witi. enthusiasm ; then the Mackenzies drove horn:, to Rockmount and Kenneth put his aunt an. cousin into the Alandale carriage, Mr. Arnb, accompanying them. Thee: when the Eat was alone with John Leigh and his lawyer h, knew that the moment had come tor a ful diSclosure of all that they could tell him. - " All I entreat is that you tell me, every- thing and keep back nothing.".• , Sir John Leigh was the first to speak. NlorNtVohno. discovered red t wattmurderer o criminal, but .a young man whose he ant errdeer o ; n c prospects had . been wrecked and his Ultolt character perverted by a woman's falseness. When Helen Jardine left; Australia she •wa, RiChlatrdwas actually engaged to this Gresham and hat promised to-Inarry him on his return from sea He was absent with his ship when she heart. of her changed fortune and she sailed for Eng- land without writing a line to tell him of he' plans or even saying good-bye .to his motile] who lived in Melbourne. "Of course there may have been excuses for Miss Jardine, but so far as I know thE story it runs thus, that being riah .she liberately forsook the lover of her poorer days and left him in blank ignorance -of her -destina- tion. "That her desertion was Greshane; ruin l

have ample proof; he tracked her to Thornb and followed in pursuit ; he witnessed one o: her secret meetings with Norton, and—tht rest you know. " I don't want to say one harsh word of you: cousin,. but I can't help feeling Gresham ww hardly used. Anyway, when he was flying, promised him he should see her once agait and I kept my word. " He died while she was with him and then is no doubt the meeting greatly distressed her. but I do not believe there was a thought it] • her mind when she left tile court of not re• turning to the Hall. She was wearing a thii; summer dress and a big picture hat, not in d&. least the costume in which anyone Nvouiti start on a long night journey." Alandale's heart ached. HOW well he remem. bered that dress and its sweet fugitive per: fume of violets ! As he mused •he seemed tc see again • the bare whitewashed walls of Ills prison rooms and the beautiful face of the girl he had held in his arms. And she was lost, the one" love of his life had - gone out into the w ild world a lonely fugitive I " Jack, I --don't want to seem ungrateful," he said hoarsely, " but you don't know what it means to me. I laved her so—she loved me, too, and when once I heard that' Ti was free my first thought, was that we migfit be happy together. Black as your story paints Helen, I believe there must be some excuse for her if only we could find it out ; perhaps she wrote to Gresham and the letter missed him at some foreign port, or perhaps she was drawn into the engagement against her will. I am sure of one thing, she never loved him and it was not her wealth that parted •them." L "Keen your faith in her if you can," said

div.head: DON'T NEGLECT YOUR SKIN!
div.p: DON'T NEGLECT YOUR SKIN!
GOLF.
home, then I took it out and looked at tne envelope—the writing Was Helen's, she was alive.

" I tore the letter to fragments unread, but I never doubted the truth. Helen was alive and before she returned to claim her inherit- ance her supplanter must be gone. "You will never see my face again, for all time I shall be as dead' to you as though the grave had already closed over me. I entreat you by the love you once Ipore me forgive my sin and think- as kindly as you can of the sinner."

div.head: CHAPTER XXVIII
div.p: CHAPTER XXVIII

LORD ALANDALE said nothing to Lady Mary or Magdalen ~Of the letter .he had received from • his lost love; he • would gladly have stayed away from the Hall for an indefinite period, so intensely painful was the subject of the miss- ing girl to him, but Lady Mary sent such piteous notes, begging him to come to her that two days after his return •to Woodlands he forced himself to walk up the familiar avenue cad .suffer fqiles to usher him into his aunt's sitting-r00m... To 11;7, dismay she looked terribly worn and ill. Reluctantly Kenneth began to realise that he had not been the only one to suffer. in the last feifi weeks; the strain and anxiety of the lOtig Orawn out Suspense had in homely phrase "Made an old woman" of Lady Mary, and the discovery_ gave the Earl a great
to I;ear with-her laments.

:Ezit. to his surprise his aunt 'spoke very qmetly and reasonably ; perhaps she guessed how much abUse of the lost heiress tried Islcane,th, for what she said was that for Mag- (l7.!en's sal:e it was imperative the question IK; sot at rest ; if indeed she whom they ttcid called Helen Jardine had no right to the viy then Magdalen was even now the -410,fni mistress of Mondale. " Magdalen is young and may marry some day," remarked Lady Mary. "I never liked her mother, but her father was my •own brother and I will not see his child wronged." " Aunt Mary," said Lord Alandale, I will pledge you my solemn word that in a month from this time Magdalen shall have her rights, if rights indeed are hers. Will that content

yOI ? . " suppose it must, but I can't think limy you will manage to work it, Kenneth. tr. Fielding told me he had employed one of The ablest 'detectives of the day, to trace that unfortunate girl, but 'all trace of her had vanished

Lord Alamlale winced at the adjective ap- to his poor love. " I do not pledge myself to produce Helen," HP said gravely, "only to solve all doubt as to ?agdalen's position, to settle the question whether she is or is not the heiress of our house "

" Will you not see Magdalen before you ? " pleaded Lady Mary as he rose to take leave of her. "She is your own cousin and vou have been the best of friends all your lives, why should you turn against her now? I dare not stay any longer," replied Lord Alendale," for I want if possible to catch the live o'clock train to Loudon. .Aunt Mary, try not to worry more than you can help. I believe the tangle will smooth out straight yet." " And you believe in her, Kenneth.? You are ' No need to ask to whom the prononn re- ferred. Lord Alandale sighed heavily. " At least leave me in my 'blindness, Aunt Mary, do not try to shake my faith. ;This eeich I will tell you and believe that I speak the truth, whether the 'girl you so condemn is I bleu Jardine or Hildred jasper makes no diUcrence to the fact that she is, she will ever be, the one. love of my heart." lie went ont leaving Lady Mary in tears. Ile met I.lls cousin Magdalen in the long avenue leading down to the lodge, and in spite of his haste he paused to take her hand in " I ati. going to London, Magda, and I can't tell wheiNl shall be back. ' For the sake of the old childish days when we were such good friends I want you to ,do use one, favour, stay ‘vith my aunt for at least a Month:" Magdalen looked astonished. "'Let, Kenneth, mother has gone home to Kew and she is beginning to grumble at being left so long," " Magda," said Lord Alandale very gently, "I ask my favour for My own sake and Aunt Mary's, but also, just a little, for yours. My clear, gos Sip travels very swiftly. Depend upon it very soon your mother will learn the cruel theory which Aunt Mary has 'invented about —abeut poor Helen ; after that what will your life at Mew he like until it is settled beyond a question who is the heiress of Alandale ?,' ii ;daler. was quick to understand. " I see what you mean, Kenneth, and I will promise to stay here a full month." " " God bless you, Magda, now and ever." Oh I Kenmeth." and a sort of choked .) fjnoetl-rrike off her words. " After all, \\*lint does it matter who has the legal claim to Al:teldele. If it is Htlen's really, well and ; if not, why not let it still be called hers ? if it werpri mine should give it back to you end, you will marry her, so that either way the result will be the same and she will be • mistress here." "le\nd do you think would take such a gilt' from you, Magda ? " " I think you ought to let me have my way."

And how about your husband ? " I shall never have such a possession. iie7ietli, • since we are talking so seriously, pc:nzips I had better tell you the trtith.; whenever my Mother's death sets me free to .cluiose my (7,Wu life r shad take the veil and become a Sister of. the Anzlican Church." "Magda! " "It is. a , great secret,: only somehow ': I wanted you. to know. If if. turns out that Alandale is mine, I shall execute a legal deed renouncing all claim to it in your favour:" " It is a generous thought, but, Magda, I explain my words. You must not ask me a Lingle, quition, but in My heart I am , convinced of this: Alandale, is neither yours nor mine." A few directions at Woodlands, and Lord Alandale drove to the station ; after all, he did not go to London that night, but alighted at York, for he had come to that pass when he, felt he must have the advice of a faithful fri(ml/and he could trust Joe Fielding through and through, knowing that even though Joe did •n6t like or trust the lost 'Helen he would give his advice candidly and fairly. Dinner was over when the Earl reached Mr. Fielding's Louse '; his friend received him in the study and after pressing refreshments upon him in vain sat down to await his conildenee. ' " Fielding, it is not a' lawyer's advice but a friclvi's • I want to-night, and what passes between us must not travel beyond this roo:71.."

" Right." " You Imow xy aunt's amiable theory about —Hulett ? " • • " Yes." " Supposing it were true ill part. that bite girl we knew as rAy cousin was really Hildred Jasper l•ut the true Helen Jardine was still alive, might not tile letter of which I have heard so much have come from her and been to te;l her friend that she had come back, as it were. from the grave ? " Joe looked thoughtful. " There are only two .theories that will adMit of this seuond girl being alive. If she had been saved i fOIll the sinking boat she.. would have claimed her rights lcng ago, unless--" 1' Go on," said Alandale. " I'vethonght it all out tor myself but I want your opinion,

too." " She might have met with such injuries as resulted in brain fever," said Joe thought- fully, " and sometimes I have heard of suspended memory following a terrible shock She might have kept.. silent all this time just because she had forgotten her own identity." " And yo);r other idea? " "1 don't dknow--bu t she would be young and pretty, possibly romantiz. What is to have prevented her falling in love with some- one who shared her perils and keeping her real name from him—on account of Charles Gresham ? " • " Joe—I believe you've hit it. I am positive my cousin Helen Jardine is alive, . and that she wrote the letter which sent--
the ' other girl away from AlandaleJ tell me, how am I to find her ? " Meaning the real • Helen Jardine ? _ .

" Judging from the latitude it which the, 'Cygnet • took fire it seems likely that her boats would drift off the Italian coast, and anc, We know; reached Genoa. The par- ticular boat in Which the young lady was sank, but she may have been rescued by sonic:: trading ship. The chief trade of Italy and Sicily is in wines, marble, and preserved fruit. I should say go to Palermo and make cautious- caiquiries." "And you think—" " I think you may find a clue to all lint puzzles ydu, but—you will get the explanation though more slowly if you stay at home, for, believe me, if Helen Jardine is in Sicily, and wrote that letter, finding it unanswered, slie• will surely write again." But Lord Alandale's mind was made up. "I shall go to London by the night mail and travel overland to Naples; from there it will be easy enough to get a boat to Palermo.'

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH.

lIXITED BAND OD HOPE INTKETENG.—The concluding Pileating in connection with Hill Cliff° and Stockton ,eath United Band of Hope, was held in the new 'iyesleyan Schoolroom, Stockton Heath on Monday. T h° Rev. J. S. Huges presided over a large attendance. After the Chairman's address the Temperance Queen (Miss ;resale Ellison), with guards, maids of honour, train-bearers, &c., proceeded to occupy the position of honour on the platform. The first part of the programme consisted of the temperance cantata " Slaves or free," which was well given by about 50 members of the Band of-Hope who had been trained by Mrs. Davenport, Br. E. Ellison acting as conductor, and Master Whitfield as organist. The second part of the programme was opened by the "Queen's speech" a pretty and effective address being delivered by MiSF Ellison. By the permission of the Warrington Band of }lope Union, several drills, solos and action songs, were given with great success, each item being encored. Special mention should be made of the action duet, " don't want to play in your yard," by Elsie Whitfield and Dolly Cain, the actions of this and" Creepmouse " by infant girls were exceedingly well given. Miss May Isherwood was beard to advantage in her song " The woodland madrigal," and in response to an encore gave " Time's roses (the test piece at the recent Leigh Eisteddfod, at which she secured the first prize). A bar bell drill, by a team of boys trained by Miss Jackson ret,, also well given. During the eventng over ,10.certi- ates of merit were awarded to members of good s,ttendance, &c., and a book prize to Master Ernest Whitfield for ticket selling. A vote of thanks to all ‘sho had taken part was accorded on the proposition of r. G. Whitfield, seconded by Mr. H. Breretoo. Miss ''..ernas, Mrs. Stevenson, and Master Whitfield acted as "ecompanists.

div.head: RUGBY UNION.
div.p: RUGBY UNION.
THE FREE CHURCHES.
THE NATIONAL FREE CHURCH COUNCILi

The issue of a special number of the 7ree Church Chronicle, devoted to an account of the meetings of the National Free Church Council at Birmingham, brings once more into promi,- nenee the great parliament of the Free Churches which closed its sessions so recintly. Full reports have appeared in 'religious and secular papers, but the topics that were brought into prominence in those few days are still excit- ing considerable attention. Many opinions on the meetings are given in this ' special issue of the Chronicle. The President, for 'in- stance, thus records his impreSsions :—" It is matter for the, deepest thankfulness that the meetings of the Council at Birmingham were so successful, not only from the point of view of attendance, but by reason of the spiritual power which marked many of them. Several features will remain permanently stamped upon my mind. In the first place, the outstanding excellence and deep influence of the sermons preached before the Council. Dif- ferent as they were in type and tone of thought, one grace was manifest in them all. Another event 'which I shall always bear in thankful recollection was the endorsement; given by the vast audience to my expression' to Mr. Crooks, M.P., Of the de- termination of Free Churchmeit throughout the country to assist the representatives of labour in seeming more human conditions for the poor and suffering classes of the nation. The dis- cussion on open-air preaching, by its earnestness and ability, gave great promise of a wide exten- sion of this most necessary forth of evangelism, while the responsiveness of the Council to the Devotional Addresses was a happy augur Y of spiritual revival."

div.head: WOMEN'S MEETING.
div.p: THE WOMEN'S MEETING.

One of the engagements of the National Council was a meeting exclusively for women, when Mrs. Bendel Harris occupied the chair, and speeches were (riven- by Lady Halliwell Rogers, Mrs. Caine, t'Mrs. Burnett Smith, and Mrs. Charlotte -Benham. A male reporter in the 'Free Church Chronicle gives his impressions of a feminine audience :—" The atmosphere of the meeting was one of great quietness. NO one seemed to move or to whisper. The ladies, apparently, have only one method of applause— the hand-clap. Not a single "Hear, hear" broke the silence of the meeting. No one shouted "Hurrah!" No one stamped on the floor or rustled feet. One of the speakers sakl her time was up and she must leave off, and the audience, instead of saying,- Go on ! " as the delegates said many times during the National Council, only clapped! When some pathetic tales were brought out by one of the speakers, the audience did not cry "Shame ! —they each one looked at her neighbour with a book that had to convey what speech had not yet invented an expression for."

div.head: NEW PRESIDENT.
div.p: THE NEW PRESIDENT.

The Rev. J. Scott Lidgett, M.A., the new President, created a very favourable impression. It is stated that Mr. Lidgett will make a hard- working tind thorough President, and his year of office should be of great service to the movement. He has already started on his Presidential Campaign. He intends visiting most, if not all, of the District Federations, and he is going to crowd into one day as much work as it is possible to sustain. His day's meetings will include a Conference at eleven o'clock, public luncheon at one o'clock, business meeting at 2.30, a sermon at four o'clock, ,public tea at 5.15, and a demonstration at seven or eight o'clock—truly a comprehensive and. exhaustive programme for one day. It is understood that Mr. Lidgett will, in the Con- ferences, deal with social and religious questions of importance, and will endeavour to stir up the Free Church Councils to fresh endeavour in Social Service. •

div.head: FREE CHURCH YEAR BOOK.
div.p: FREE CHURCH YEAR BOOK.

There has been anxiety in many quarters to get the text of some of the excellent papers delivered at the National Free Church Council. Dr. Forsyth's luminous paper, for instance, on "The Place of Spiritual Experience in the maLing of Theology" had to be cut down in delivery owing to the time-limit, and Dr. Hanson's paper on "The Necessity for Open-air Preaching" had to be omitted at the Sessions, owing to that .gentle- man, being called away at -the time of the delivery. These papers, together with all the other sermons and addresses, are given in full in the official record of the meetings, which is to_ be published in the "Free Church Year Book," 1906 edition.

div.head: IMPORTANT FEATURES.
div.p: IMPORTANT FEATURES.

This . Year Book has now become indis- pensable to Free Churchmen. It, is every year made more comprehensive, and, in addi- tion to the Official Report of /the Birming- ham meetings and a full record :of the Work of the year of the National and Local Councils, valuable information is given which Free Churchmen cannot afford to miss. The sta- tistics of the year are given as usual. They show considerable increase over those of last year, owing, to some 'etent, to the revival in Wales, which has meant great Accession to the ranks. of the Churches.' FEL CHURCHES ON THE MISSION FIELD.

A valuable table is given showing the position of the Free 'Churches on • the Mission Field, the number of missionaries employed by the various societies, the number of stations, tiunday-school scholars, c., also the National and internatioval figures on the same field. . A short summary shows the position of the Free. Churches .with regard to the temperance . movement. . Then the history of the various denominations in England is given concisely and accurately. A. digest of the law as it affects Free Churches and Free Churchmen, a list of the Free Church Members of Parlia- ment, full lists of, Training Colleges open to Free Churchmen,. Ministerial ,Colloges, Settle- ments, Organisations, &c., a list of Free Church Councils and Secretaries-4—these are Some of the other Heins in the Year Boob. In spite of the constant addition to its pages, the price of the Year Book remains the same, as. id., and published by the National Free Church Council.
DISESTABLISHMEN.T FOR WALES.

One of the measures which are expected at an early date from the new Government, is the disestablishment of the ChurCh in Wales. A resolution on this subject was passed at the Birmingham Free Church meetings. In the Free Church .Chronicle for April a historical sketch of the movement for disestablishinent in Wales is given which will be read with great interest.

div.head: FREE cIIUMH WORK IN ARMY AND NAVY.
div.p: FREE cIIUMH WORK IN ARMY AND NAVY.

The Rev. E. P. Lowry, whose name has been in the papers quite recently in connec- tion with an incident of the Basingstoke by- election, is one of the leading Wesleyan Chap- lains at Aldershot. Mr. Lowry, who is quite an authority' on the subject, has written in this months issue of the Free Churchman an article on "Free Church Work in Army and Navy." It shows what means are taken to spiritually pare for the increasing number of soldiers who are free Churchmen.

difficulty thereby overcome. He was sorry to notice how high the death rate was. It seemed to be higher than the average for the 76 large towns and the 141 smaller towns. They could not really feel quite setisaed with resnits like that though he dirt not think it was the fault of Dr. Gornall who, he thought, waS doing all he possibly could to improve the sanitary conditions in the town. The committee were also doing their share but they must not rest upon their oars so long as the statistics were so iinfavouraible. It was especially lamentable to notice the extremely high rate of child I mortality. It was enough to make a sympathetic ' citizen weep to see the terrible hecatomb of children, doe largely to ignorance on the part of the parents. The Sanitary works Committee were rather proud of the way in which the sewers were flushed, but if they possessed his nose and lived in his neighbourhood he thought their transports would be somewhat mediflod. With regard to the smoke nuisance he noticed that Dr. Gornall •ventured upon a rather caustic criticism of their neglect in that respect. The nuisance had been stopped at the electrical works. He did not suggest that manufacturers should be prosecuted, but rather , took the view of the Beautiful Warrington Society that they should be pitied and taught the harm which they were doing and what slims of money were wasted by , allowing the dense smoke to escape. Cooneillor CHANTLEIZ asked for a legal opinion as to the alcohol placard. He had no personal objection to it. It ores the abuse of alcohol not the use, that did the harm. The use was all right if they would ouly take the aleehol regularly and do as they should. (Loud laughter). The MAYOR: Do you mean as far as the expense is concerned ? The placard will not do much harm or much good. (Laughter). I was asked to put my name to it, but I think the Health Committee should take the responsibility of it. Councillor C.:LAWLER : Are,they willing to be sur- charged. The MAYOR : They ought tlo**be if' they are not. (Laughter). The DEPUTY Tows CLERK : They have a perfect right to spend the money if they like, because they are doing so for the promotion of thehealth of the borough. It may bright or it may be wrong,but it is the opinion of the Health Committee that they are doing good to the borough. Councillor CITANTLER : This is an object lesson: If we don't put our foot down we shall have the vegetar- ians and anti-vaccinators requiring placards to be issued at our expense. Let them be put up at their own expense, and not at the expense of the ratepayers of Warrington. At Birmingham the Connell were surcharged by the Local Government Board. There is a difference of opinion about this question. The MAYOR : Will you propose that the resolution be struck out? Councillor CFLANTLER : I enter a protest. The -DEPUTY TOWN CLERK : The issuing of the placard is perfectly legal. I\never heard of a Corpora- tion being surcharged. Councillor CIIANTLER : They (the temperance party) are in a minority,but t is the majority that rule in this country. The MAYOR The people it is meant for will never relad the placard because they will have had too much alcohol. and will not see it. (Laughter.) That is the only class it is intended to catch. This is only a fad of someone. Alderman TINNION said that as a teetotaler it seemed ' to him that the Mayor's own reflection was a justitioa- tion for the action of the Committee its deciding to issue the placard. (Hear, hear.) Councillor Ettisos would have no objection if a similar handbill was circulated in every house in the borough. (Hear, hear.) Councillor WILKINSON explained that the question of the placard had been taken into careful consideration and it was not the moderate drinker that was aimed at. A sovereign would cover the whole expense of the issu- ing of the placard. He was s )rry that the opposition had come from the source which it had mod thought it would have been better if Councillor Chantler had got someone to raise the objection to the placard and not have raised it himself. Couucillor CIIANTLI6R : I would rather do my own work myself. The minutes were approved. NECESSARY OR UNNECESSARY?

A resolution of the Sanitary Works Committee, pro- posing to roof with glass a convenience at the end of Bewsey-road, raised a lengthy discussion. An amend- menty Councillor Lord, seconded by for the abolishing of the conveni- cenocneei wasoaltogether. moved Pemberton • Eventually it was decided to carry out the Committee's proposal.

MAYOR'S AUDITOR. The MAYOR announced that he had appointed Council- lor Wilson as his auditor for the ensuing year. EDUCATION COMMITTEE'S RECOM- • MENDATIONS; . -SELECTED MEMBERS WITHDRAWN.

Alderman BENNETT moved the confirmation of the recommendations of the Educatioh Committee that Mrs. Jane H. Edelsten and Mr. A. J. Jolley be appointed as selected members of the Education Committee. He thought the Committee had been magnanimous in listening to th,e wishes of the Town Council in appoint- ing a lady. - Coquetllor LORD asked, if the recommendation was in order as it had not been placed on the minutes of the Education Committee. Several members of the Council not knowing the question was coming up left the meet- ing of the Committee to attend to other Committee meetings. The MAYOR said that according to the standing orders of the Education, Committee the matter would have to be put upon the agenda paper. Councillor LORD moved as an amendment that the minute be referred back. The matter was out of order and further he thought they ought to have selected an economist instead of Mr. A. J. Jolley. They had been working on lines of economy and he thought an economist ought to be appointed. Councillor PEMBERToN seconded. Alderman BENNET:L. said the matter was brought for- ward in absolute good faith and with a desire to pro- mote the efficient working of the Education Committee and with a view to completing the constitution of the Committee as early as possible. The fact that members of the Council absented themselves from the work of the Committee had been the cause of a great deal of trouble in the past. But if they thought it well that the committee should pursue its work without two members he withdrew the minute. Councillor PEMBERTON did not think it fair that Alderman Bennett should use the remark which he had. He wasat the Committee meeting and on that particular day was at the Town Hall for six hours. It was unfair that Alderman Bennett should accuse the members of the Council as they did not know the matter was being brought forward. - Alderman BENNETT withdrew the recommendation with reference to the staffing of the schools. He understood that strong exception was taken to the minute and in accordance with a request from the Mayor he withdrew it though he really thought it was a wise, sound and moderate one. There was no reason, however, why the newly constituted School Manage- ment Committee should not re-consider the matter though he thought they would come to the same con- clusion as tke old Committee. , Councillor CLEGG raised the question of the teachers obtaining certificates for giving physical instruction but was inforrned that the Council has no right to discuss the (region. Alderman rINNION said he was going to raise the same question. He considered the certificates granted by the Warrington Gymnasium Instructor to be equal or probably superior to any certificate given by a local 1 education authority. The minutes were approved. PUBLIC HEALTH. THE ABUSE OF ALCOHOL. PLACARD ISSUED BY THE COMMITTEE. The Health Committee recommended the adoption of a resolution forwarded by the Chester City Council- calling for the amendment of the Canal Boats Act and the Education Acts, in order that children on canal boats might be brought under the compulsory attendance clauses of the Education Acts. At the same meeting of the Committee the Medical Officer submitted information which he had obtained from other towns in reference to the isolation of oases of phthisis. It was resolved that application be made to the Local Government Board to include phthisis in the list of notifiable diseases. It was also ref (dyed that the following placard as to the abuse of alcohol be issued in the form of the draft subruittedaby the Medical Officer of Health. "The abuse of alcohol aud its evil consequences. Evidence as to the enormous amount of damage done directly and indirectly to men and women by the abuse of alcohol, is apparent in every town. The Health Committee desires to draw attention to this as one of the important causes in lowering the health of the people and rendering them easily suscept- ible to ninny diseaset. The report of the committee on physical degeneration presented to Parliament by com- mand of His Majesty the King, calls the attention to ' the following facts :—I. The abuse of alcoholic stimu- lants in form of either beer, wine or spirits is a most potent and deadly agent of physical deterioration. 2. Alcoholic persons are specially liable to consumption and all other inflammatory disorders. 3. A consider- able number of men and women become insane as the result of the abuse of alcohol. 4. Drinking babies among women are increasing, and these habits are very prejudical to their offspring, idiocy, epilepsy,and other diseases carry them off, and too frequently the squalid epoivledrrteyn:b 5. It was resolved that , the request be granted, and that the Town Council be recommended to petition Parlia- ment in favour of the removal of the existing embargo on the importation of live Canadian cattle into Great Britain. Councillor EVANS, in moving the confirmation of the minutes, said that with reference to children on canal boats very few children would be affected in the War- rington area, but at the same time it was felt desirable that the resolution should be supported. Phthisis, it had been found, was one of those diseases which was making extraordinary progress, and was giving very serious trouble to health authorities all over the country. So far as Warrington was concerned, there were at present about 400 cases, and about 100 deaths occurred , from thedisense every year. It was the intention of the I Health Committee to experiment upon the disease by the isolation of one or two cases taken from places where the surroundings were not favourable to the recovery of the patients. With refers nce to the placard which the committee proposed to issue, i... was not issued from any particular teetotal ideas but with a considera- i tion for the health of the town. The important points raised in it were the outcome of an inquiry by the king 1 into physical degeneration. With reference to the importation of cattle it was felt that the embargo ; should be removed and that young cattle should be imported and fed in England for the market. Canadian , cattle were selected because it was a rare thing for any of them to be affected by tuberculosis. Councillor BURTON seconded. ALDELIMA.N BENNETT AND THE MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.

div.p: THE STATE OF PARR STREET'. -

Councillor CHANTLEit called the attention of the Paving and Sewerage Committee to the state of Parr- street. Residents in that district were beginning to think that the Corporation were wilfully delaying the work. Other streets could receive immediate attention whereas the residents in Howley had to live in a perfect quagmire and up to their necks in "slutch." THE HIRING 010 THE PARR HALL. When the minutes of the Town Hall, Parks and Baths Committee were under consideration, Councillor MAGINN said a letter had been put into his hand regard- ing the amount which the St. Mary's Dramatic Society were charged for the use of the Parr Hall. 1 Councillor Maginn was, ruled out of order by the MAYOR, who said the question was one for the General I Purposes Committee to consider. Councillor MAGEOT questioned and for a time declined to obey the Mayor's ruling,,and only resumed his seat I when the Council declined to allow him to proceed.

div.head: CORPORATION AND THE RIVER.
div.p: CORPORATION AND THE RIVER.

The MAYOR informed the Council of the judgment with reference to costs in the Ship Canal. action, The Corporation, he said, had managed to get their costs out of the Ship Canal Company. (Hear, hear). Alderman SMETHURST called attention to the Rivers Committee's estimate of -2220 as expenditure for the co.ming:vear, and asked what it was for.

The'l‘ls:voft : Wages. Alderinan SMETHERST : But is this Corporation paying wages for the river to be looked after for the traders ? don't see why we should pay. The MAyort : It is the same as you paid your officials last year. They look after the river to get more trade, and thus more rates for the borough. Alderman SMETHURST : We :ire • paying 2220. for doing someone else's work. - The matter then dropped. THE TRAMS. FREE PASSES, OFFICIALS AND THEIR TRAMFARES. LIVELY DISCUSSION. • At, a meeting of the Electricity and Tramways Com- mittee held on the :27th March it was resolved that on and after the Ist April next no free passes be issued for use on the tram cars, and that tokens be issued to par- sons holding such passes on payment at the same rate as Corporation Departments. Alderman SMETHURST, in moving the adoption of the proceedings of the Electricity and Tramways Committee which included the above resolution, remarked that he had done all he conld to prevent it, but he was in a minority. Councillor Magian was the father of the resolution and Councillors Lord, Pemberton and Wilkinson supported it. He was against it. He would now like to "reply. vit the Council's permission, to a letter which appeared in the papers Councillor Pemberton : If the letter appeared in the papers Alderman Smethurst should answer it in the papers. me Coencil declined to allow Alderman Smethurst to reply to the letter and the Alderman resumed his seat. Conncillor WILKINSON seconded. The object of their action with reference to free passes was to ventilate the subject and to see how far the officials were taking 1 advantage of free riles on the cars. Councillor ManINN : I have been reading the resolu- tion for the last ten minutes and I admit I am dense —(laughter)--but I hope there is somebody in this Council, who is not so dense as I am, who will under- stand it, for I am hanged if I can understand it. (Laughter.) He was the father of the resolution, he I continued, and he intended to have attention while it I was discussed._ No one, whether servants of the Council or anyone else, would in future ride on the cars without I paying. They had been told that some people had done I good for the town. Quite so, but did those people accept their positions for the s. the benefit of I themselves or simply the benefit of the town ? He held they accepted them for the 2 s. d., and they should pay their transfares the same as anybody else—and they were well able to do so. (Hear, hear.) For some time there Ind been an influence at work in Stockton Heath —a part of the town which was not a part of the town. (Laughter.) There were some people there prepared to I ,I call themselves Warrington people when it cost them ' nothing and to deny Warrington if it should cost them anything. "Phere were certain officials drawing the I money of the town, but the town was not good enough for them to live in, so they went to Stockton Heath— I and the Corporation paid for trams to carry them there. He was surprised that the officials did not go to live at cKanrurytsfotrhdemandHe thaesriO. thatthe as surprised Corporation t shouldthe humbleness of their claim. He heard of one I great official drawing about £4OO a year from the Cor- poration who had threatened that he would resign rather , than live in the town. Still he was glad to thaw his I 2400 a year from" dirty Warrington." (Laughter.) If he Councillor Maginn) had his way he would say that no man should draw a salary from the borough and not live and pay rates in the borough, but, of course, that was too big s thing for the Council to take in one swallow. (Laughter). Wages were just the same from I the Corporation as from Bewsey Forge, or Monks's. Those employes had to pay their tram fares and Cor- poration officials should pay. (Hear, hear,) Their work began when they got to the office, and the Cor- poration ought not to have to pay to get them there. Councillor PEMBERTON said he had often been charged with pandering to the ,atepayers but it was worse that a gentleman should pander to the officials. Alderman SMETHURST : I have not. Councillor PENIIinitTON said the officials who had caused this matter to be raised were drawing their hundreds and were well able to pay. He did not go sit far as Councillor Maginn, although there was no doubt it would be to the advantage of Corporation under- takings if the officials did live in the town. div.head: GARDE REPUBLICAINE RAND_
div.p: GARDE REPUBLICAINE RAND_

The "Daily Mirror" recently published a photograph depicting one of the most interesting incidents of the visit of the Garde Republicaine Band to London. it showed this famous musical combination making records for talking rnachires in the recording laboratory of the Columbia Phonograph Company iii Grit Eastern Street. It is generally recognized that the Garde Republicaine Band occupies a positdon of pre-eminence among military bands. Our own King., indeed, is reported to have expressed to the French Ambassador his opinion that this celebrated bsnd is the lidest in the world. it is signincant testimony, therefore, to the high level of efficiency attained in the talking machine industry that a musical organization of such renown should be willing to commit its credit to talking machine records. There is practicaßy no risk, however, in entrusting even the most distinguished reputation to , Columbia records. Past signal successes amply demonstrate this. Those who heard the Garde IRepublicaine Band during its recent visit he this ' country will not soon forget the musical treat they then enjoyed. They will now be able to repeat that treat at will, by means of the Columbia records; while 'those who' were unable to attend any of the performances in London will be able to remedy their loss by making the acquaintance of the band through the medium of the gramophone. A list of the Garde Republicaine Records—for both cylinder and disc tatki,g machines— is included in the April Supplement to "Price Book 20" issued h 7 The Columbia Phonograph Company, General, 89, Great Eastern-street, London E.C. A post card request will bring it to any of our readers by return of post.
WIRRAL AND BIRKENHEAD AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY'S SHOW.-CEIANGE OF DATES.

In consequence of the Council receiving notice of the Liverpool RACPS being filed to take place on the dates selecterl for this Society's annual show, a special meet- ing of the Council has unanimously agreed it would he most unwise to hold.the show on the same days as the Liveopool Race Meeting,there fore that July 18th and 19th ,be adopted as the dates for this year's Show instead of July 25th and 26th as previously announced.

COMMER6IAL FAlLURES.—According to " Remp's Mercantile Gazette," the total number of Commercial Failures recorded in England and Wales during the week ending 'Friday, March 30th, was 179, viz. :—New Bankruptcy Proceedings published in the London i Gazette, 39; Deeds of Arrangement registered,9o. The ! respective numbers in the corresponding week of last year were : Bankruptcies, 100 ; Deeds of Arrangement, 90—total 190 ; being a decrease of 17. The total num- ber of Commercihl ' Failures recorded during the 13 weeks of the present year is 2,230 ; the total number recorded in the corresponding 13 weeks of last year was 2,442, showing a decrease of 203. •

div.head: BOARD OF GUARDIANS D. Braide and the Board's Action. " Exceeding their Powers."
div.p: BOARD OF GUARDIANS D. Braide and the Board's Action. " Exceeding their Powers."

A.meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardians was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday, Mr. J. Billinge. presiding. There were also present :—Mrs. Clay, Mrs. Wilkinson. Dr. Patterson, Dr. Murray, Messrs. W. Hickman, J. W. Knowles, A. Brooks, G. Thompson. T. Ritchie, S.'Davies, Payton,T. Ll.?;shcroft, R. Bolton, NT. W. Seton, W. Houghton, J. Cook, G. Mather,'R, Flannagan, J. 0: Sutton (clerk!. J.. F. Awbery (master), A. Wright (supprintendent of Padgate Schools). HOUSE COMMITTEE'S BUSINESS. At a meeting of this House Comrnitte- on March 23rd, the annual roll call of men resulted in 23 being called upon to take their discharge on various dates. The committee dealt with the protest made by the medical (Wiper as to the .absence of an alternative escape in base of fire in the old hospital buildings which urn to be used to relieve the overcrowding in the female hospital. The Master was instructed to make a flat concrete roof in place' of the present slate roof and tqprovide an external 'staircase of wood and to pur- eiase any materials necessary to effect the carrying out of the additional safeviatd. At a subsequent meeting it was .resolved that Frei Clare be appointed labour master at a salary of £3O a year with he usual emolutnents. . The minutes were approved. VACCENATIoN CHARGES. _

A letter was read from the Leigh Guardians suggest- in," that a conference of ;Boards'of Gitardians shonld be held to consider the question of vaccination charges. Mr. JOLLEY moved that the letter should lie on the table. Mr. Ttronrscre thought the Board ought to take all ' action passible with a view to reducing expenditure on vaccination and be proposed that the letter he enter- tained. There were several points they had to con- sider in regard tp vaccination. First there was the very great expense. Then he considered the present system a great hardship to medical men generally. Why should the Board bring a doctor from a certain part of the district and pay him three half-crowns when they had a, doctor on the spot who could do it for half-a- crown? The ratepayers were suffering heavily through the vaccination charges which were enormous. Mr. ASHCROFT seconded. .7krr. BROOKS seconded Mr. Jolley' proposal, pointing out that he sympathised with Mr. Thompson's views bet as long as the Poor Unions Law Association had the matter in hand he thought it would be better to leave that body to deal with it instead of sending resolutions from isolated Boards of Guardians, Mr. ,JoLLEtr expressed similar views, observing that he thought the atteupt to secure fresh legislation would he more effectual if it came through the Poor Law Unions Association. Mr. TllO-APSON 'withdrew his amendment and the Board agreed that the letter should lie on the table.

DR. naAtflE AND THE DOA RD. The CLERK road a letter addressed to hiro by Dr. Braids in the corms of which he said :-I,te the resole- ; tion passed by the Board at the last meeting referring toy attendance at the Workhouse, I have been advised that in passing such a resolution the Guardians are exceeding their powers. While I remain Medical Officer : at the Workhouse I intend to go whenever sent for to ; urgent cases, and to pay my usual daily visits as hitherto,. staying until my work is finished and then leaving. It is absurd to ask me to stay two hours each morning. I Mr. .TOLEv thollfztat that a letter written in that tone i was a deliberate defiance of a deliberate decision of the : Board, and should not be lightly passed over. Heruayed that the Nfaster be instructed to convenes special meet- ing of the House Committee to be held on Friday tcr ' consider the matter. ' Mr. FOnSITAW seconded.... . . .
----- Mr . THOMPSON seggested that the matter should he deferred for the new House committee to deal with after the anneal meeting of the Board had been held.

y, • to, • Mr. KYowt,Es agreed with Mr, Thompson. His Vi3Vir about the letter was that the doctor was right arid the committee wrong. He thought the doctor could defy them and if they reported it to the Local Government Beard he believed that authority would sag the .doctor VMS perfectly right. Dr. Braide was engaged to attend the sick people in the Infirmary and he attended them properly. When he had fitished attending them pro- perly be could go. The Board were not to say he must be there during certain hours. Mr. JOLLEY: Mr. Knowles might have incidentally remarked that the Board took the ruling e theirofficial adviser—the clerk—which is perfectly contrary to what ,Mr. Kpowles said. Mr. KNOWLES: Some people are of one mind and some of anothe;. Your clerk may be right„ but I think rain. The CLERK: What lin substance said wag that the House Committee had been charged with the manage- ment of the workhouse. It is competent for them to give any reasonable order to be attended to by any of their officers and if the officer refused to do it,. it c-ould be a question for the Local Government Hoard. I don't want it to be understood that I express any opinion as to what the Local Government Board would sty. Mr. MA:TITER.: I think the same thing has. been ' going on at Oldham and the decision of the Local Government Board was against the committee and in favour of the doctor. Mr. JOLLEY: That is a different thing. Mr. KNOWLES : We are entitled to. require the doctor to properly and efficiently attend to his work and take a reasonable time, but for the House Com- mittee to say "You are to come at nine and go at eleven"— .
Mr. JOLLEY' : They nevor said that. Mr. KNowrAs Tt amounts practically to that.

_ . After further discussion a proposal to defer the matter until the election of the new ifouse Committee was defeated and it was decided to hold a tpecial meet- ing of the committee on the subject to-day (Friday).

_ . RATES. _ The CLERK submitted for signature the calls for con- tributions by overseers to meet Union expenditure in the half-year ending at Michtelmas, 2906., prepared in accordance with the Estimates approved by the Board. It was, he stated, satisfactory to find that the low Call of sixpence in the £ in succession to calls of eightpence and sevenpence might be made.—lt was not satisfac- tory to hear from.the Lancashire County Council that a further addition of at least I,ld. in the £ to the County Call might be made.—The Rural District Coun- cil wilt reduce their calls to fonrpence in the for Public Health, Highways, and other General expendi- ture.—Beyond the advantage of the reduction of Union and District Calis of which will be Made on assess- able, being less than rateable values) material reduc- tions had been made in assessmentedof cottage properties to meet the increase in rates in the last 5 years. VOTES OF THANKS. _ -

. ...... As this was the final meeting of the Board for the year, Mr. DAVIKS moved a vote of thanks to the Chair- man for the able and impartial manner in which he had., performed the duties of his office. He spoke very highlyl of Mr. Billinge's services and said that by his tact he' had managed, on several Occasions when storms had arisen, to calm the troubled waters and save their ship, from wreck. Mr. li•7o)vt.r.s seconded, and several of the Guardians supported the motion which was heartily accorded and the chairman briefly responded, expressing his gratitude to the members of the Board and to the clerk and stair for their valuable help. • Mt. JOLLEY moved a vote of thanks to Mr. Hickman, the vice-chairman, remarking that he had shown the rugged humour of Demosthenes rather than the ponshed style of Cicero. Mr. THOMPSON secohded, and Mr. FORSRAW and the Cu AIRMAN supported the vote which was accorded_ Mr. HICKMAN responded, and said he bore towards I all his fellow members a kindly feeling although he might have an outwardly rugged mode of expression.

The Oldbury police have received information of the death of a lad named Hector Dvas (5). He was walking ing in the playground at the Causeway Green schools- and as he %Nes passing the spot where the hell is sus, pended about twenty feet from the ground, it fell upon him. The lad was struck on the-head, and was rendered unconscious. Dr. Sharpe was sent for, and deceased was taken home, where he died. The bell was being rung at the time it fell.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
APRIL 7th 1906.

A question of exceedingly THE MANUFAC- wide and deep importance TURE OF ebierged into notice for a OPINION. moment or two during question time in the House of Commons on Wednesday. Mr. HILAIILIE BELLoc, who combines great impetuousness of manner with unusual directness of speech, asked the Under-Secretary for the Colonies whether it would not be possible, seeing what the London Press is at the moment, for Government depart- ments to send round "negations of the abominable lies "published by the newspapers. Mr. HEALY hit the same nail on the head, but with more pre- cision. He wished to know whether the names of the correspondents of a famous news ageusy could not be ascertained in order that the authors of particular items of news might be identified. Replying to these inquiries, Mr. Wisrs.roN CHURCHILL confessed that in the view of the Government the matter to which they referred is serious and important. The information which is being sent to South Africa. now-a-days, he said receiving the careful consideration of his Majesty's Ministers. He added that it is an occasion of no little anxiety that the Press of the Colonies should be so largely under the influence of one particular sort of opinion, and particularly of a sort of opinion which is not predominant in this country. Even the most casual newspaper reader will be able to read between the lines in this instance. Illustrations of how opinion in this country has been misled by news from the Colonies which afterwards proved to be either wholly or partly false, will suggest themselves to his mind at once, and he may safely surmise—what is well enough known to those who give close attention to what appears in the Press, both here and elsewhere— that much of the news sent from England to our kinsfolk abroad is quite as misleading as is much of that which is supplied to ourselves from. Colonial sources. The Government has good reason to be anxious on the subject: The, recent crisis in Natal, so far as any crisis can be said to have existed, arose in the first place out . of injudicious, and, as we think, inexcusable speeches made by members or supporters of the late Government in both Houses et Parliament ; but those speeches would not have been immediately mischievous if the news sent over to South Africa in connection with the action of the Government on the subject of the twelve natives who were executed the other day had been adequate, we will not say faithful, because we do not wish to impute intention where there may only have been inadvertence. When the Lord Chancellor made his splendid reply to Lord MusEn in the House of Lords, a considerable. portion of the speech of the late High Com- missioner was sent by cable to South Africa, and only a few lines of the speech of Lord Loreburn. This is unfortunate, but easily intel- ligible. Those who sent over tbe reports of the speeches at an expense of something like 2.5. a word would naturally be anxious not to send what was not wanted. Their instinct told them which , speech would be in demand at Johannesburg. They were under no obligation to send that for which there was no market. This, without any imputation of partisanship or any unintentional unfairness, is sufficient to account for much of that mischievously imperfect information which is despatched from this country to the Colonies, and from the Colonies to ourselves. The consequences might in a very tense state of feeling be enor- mously mischievous. We cannot imagine, however, that the attention which the Government is giving to the subject Points in the direction of a censorship. Censor- ships produces greater mischiefs, as a rule, than those which they are intended to prevent. There good sense in Mr. IlEALv'a'. is really very much suggestion, the adoption of which would mean the bringing home of a responsibility which at present seems scarcely to be felt. Those who transmit news of the kind to which reference is made in these remarks, should transmit opinion as well as fact, but the opinion should not be their own. It should be expressed withia inverted commas. For their own part they should carefully dis- tinguish between news and propaganda, and were they invariably to do this, the probably unwel- come attention of the Government would not be attracted to their proceedings.

When we announced last GOOD NEWS, week that there would be no increase in the Warring- , ton rates this year we thought that such a negative gain was as much as could be expecte. But the preparation of the estimates for th various Committees showed that there ha. been a substantial saving in nearly all depar ments and the members of the Finance Co' mittee had a very pleasant and momentous- •

secret to keep to themselves during the week-end. NOTES AND NOTIONS. • On Tuesday, Alderman Fairclough announced the • good news to the Town Council and created quite ' a small sensation by the statement that there All my Eye, and Lady Mary ;as the Marquis of , would be a reduction qf fcrurpence in the rates for Graham hopes to be able to say after the poll.— the ensuing year. This was better than anyone e Punch." anticiplted and almost too good to be true.; The fact remains, however, that most of , the committees have saved money during , the past year, and nearly all have estimated their expenditure for the ensuing twelve • months at a reduced figure. Something like a proper idea of the economy which has been I : practiced in corporate affairs may be gathered from! the contemplation of the fact that but for the ! demands of the Educational Authority having j increased by 3d. in the pmnd, the total reduction ; , rates for this year would have amounted to ; 110 less than 7d. There has been, practi- • cal!Y, a saving of this amount, which is •' of cnurse largely helped by the handsome surplus ,nt £10,407 from the Gas Department. For once in a way, the ratepayers will have nothing but Praise to bestow upon the municipal authority. The lesson is apparently being taken to heart that efficiency and economy can be combined at a much lower figure than has obtained as the standard for some years past. Alderman Bennett seemed rather to fear that the best interests of the town were in danger of suffering through the insistent demand for economy, but we do not think this is at all likely to be the case. So far as we can see, the town has lost ground in only one respect, and that is in street-paving. There will certainly have to be a bio effort made by the highway department and we are glad to see that the estimates have been increased to allow for more re-paving during the ensuing year. In other respects departmental work seems to have been carried out with an efficiency which reflects the greatest credit on Committees and officials alike.

This was the congenial text ." WILY WE LOST." upon which Mr. John Whits, J.P., sermonised the Junior Conservatives with such delightful naivete on Monday evening. Probably most of them held a pretty shrewd idea that they lost because they were badly beaten by a better side. In the realms of sport this usually suffices until the opportunity for a re-trial of strength comes. But Mr. White refuses to accept a licking even by so decisive a figure as 1,500 votes, and disputes the verdict of the referee, which is never a commendable or Paying policy. In this case the referee was t°,6 great British Public, which decided Without any hesitation against Mr. White's Pusillanimous and discredited party. Now, he Says the result was " a fluke and a stake." If he had suggested that Toryism was crushed as flat as a fluke we could have under- ,St,ood him, but we see nothing fluky about that -`°oo, and the voters themselves are not of the White's that they made a mistake. Some of Mr. White's excuses are very funny. For instance he "The spurt in trade just before the election unfortunate for the Conservative party." ibtless it was, but it was very, very fortunate the country, a point which Mr. White over- •s. The Conservative party should have been assiduous in stating that trade was gone, and in the slap might not have been so painful. Iwever' Mr. White is hopeful. Manufacturers re told him the good trade would not last long, I he believes there z,re "worse times to come."lt, remarkable thing that the Conservatives have gamble for success on the chances of national 'arty. Fortunately we have a party in power !Mich takes progress RS its watchword and bases itB Own position upon the sound security of peace and plenty for all. With its meeting on Mon- THE JuNroit day evening the Junior LIBERALS. Liberal Association brought to a close a highly success- Reviewing the work which has thus tj been accomplished, it is a pleasure to be able ezNte that the Association has fully justified its isteece. Formed at a time when young men of pr I„ogressive ideas had few if any opportunities in _n:arringten for meeting for the interchange of news on great questions of the day, the organize- pon Riled a distinct want. Moteovet, it played a 6y no means unimportant part in the achieve- ment of the great victory for Free Trade and progress at the recent general election. The chief work of the Association, however, has been educe tional and there is every reason for congratulation in the fact that the members have entered with so much interest into the weekly meetings and debates. The Association has been fortunate in arranging for such an admirable series of papers, which have pointed high ideals as well as afforded an abundance of information on subjects which could not fail to be of value. Cordial thanks are due to those who have so willingly assisted the organization in its inaugural session—the first one We hope of many increasing suceessful years.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
FATALITY TO A WIDNES CAPTAIN.

James Birkenhead, captain and owner of the flat Essie lying in the Huskisson Branch Dock, Liverpool, was on Wednesday proceeding down a ladder from the quay to the flat when the ladder canted over, throwing the captain into the dock. He fell a distance of 12ft. into the water, lie was promptly got out, but on arrival nt the Northern Hospital life was found to be extinct. The deceased resided at 89, Mersey-road, Widnes.

div.head: RUNCORN MAY QUEEN FESTIVAL.
div.p: RUNCORN MAY QUEEN FESTIVAL.

The ballot for the May Queen took place at a general meeting of workers at the Mersey Mission on Thursday of last week. Six schools were represented as follows :—Parish Church, Elsie Stone, 9; St. Michael's, Gertrude Evans, 15, Holy Trinity, Martha Kilgrass, 14 ; Mersey Mission, Eliza Tonks, 14 ; Weston Church. Lily Basnett, 14; and Victoria-road Council School, Cissie Williams, 14. The result of the ballot was that Cissie Williams is to be the May Queen, Elsie Stone the lady- in-waiting, and the remainder maids of honour.

• * With the coming of the spring-like weather the demand for literature falls off. During the past few days there has been a surprising decrease in the number of books borrowed from the Warrington Library, which shows that open-air enjoyment is once more becoming the rule. * * * The swan which last season frightened some timor- ous boating people on the Dee at Chester has been drowned. It was fishing just below the old Dee Mill when its head became wedged between two stones,and in that position it was drowned. This is a sad end to an ornamental if not very useful career. * * * The rates for the borough for the ensuing year will be made up as follows : Improvement Rate 2s. The earliest date of late years upan which Easter has fallen is March 25th in 1883 and 1894. There is a dread of Easter thus synchronising with Lady-day. When our Lord falls into our Lady's lap To England will come dire misbap. The latest possible Easter-day synchronises with St. Mark's Day, April 25th. It fell then in 1736, and 150 years later, in 1886. The next " latest Easter" will be 37 years hence, in 1943. * Doctors in China evidently work on the" Kill or cure " system. * * * Alderman Bennett's hardy annual, the " smoke nuisance " was to the fore again on Tuesday. For some years the Alderman's voice has been like that of one crying in the wilderness, but he has now got valuable allies in the Medical Qfficer and the Beautiful Warrington Society, and bet Ween them we believe they will eventually do something to lessen the unnecessarily dense pall of black smoke which fre- quently overhangs the Borotmh. There is no doubt that the problem is one capable of practical solution, and if manufacturers can be persuaded to consider the " smoke nuisance " as a nuisance, and not merely as an indication or good trade, then Warrington should soon become a better place to live in. At present the atmosphere is anything but invigorating when the iron-works are in full blast. * *

Majority, lO NEGLECTING A FAMILY.

Last Thursday at Newton,Alma blanche Kelly,widow, of Suez-street, Earlestown, was charged with neglecting her four children aged from two to fifteen years.—Mr. Knowles, for the prosecution, said the facts of the case were terrible. The woman did a little charing, and was said to earn part of her living by immoral means. She had been advised to go to the workhouse, but refused, preferring her miserable state of existence, and ruining her children. The lad of 15 earned about 12s. a week which he took home to his mother, but he VMS half starved. There was hardly any furniture, and the children were allowed to "pig about." Two other sons were already in the guardians' Cottage Homes at Padgate and the woman was trying to get hold of the elder of those two, aged 14, so that he might do a little for her while she skulked about and misconducted herself. Inspector Cox N.S.P.C.C.,said he had visited the woman at three different houses since last October. lie had found the children without food, and in danger of fire. He had complaints about the woman's immorality.—P.C. Lennie gave confirmatory evidence. —Dr. Valentine deposed to examining the house and the family on Tuesday. The place and the few things in it were dirty and verminous. There were no bed-clothes. The chil- dren were aged 2, 4. and 8 years, besides the lad at work, who came in -vhile he was there, looking haggard and insufficiently fed. One of the girls also came in, with a bag of crusts, probably the result of begging.— The Bench committed the woman for three months' hard labour. SHOCKING FATALITY AT HAYDOCK. While complaining of Radical misrepresentation— that fine, broad term which includes a multitude of imaginary sins—the Conservatives do not forget to misrepresent the actions or the Government to their heart's content. Mr. Draper, who had such an unen- viable experience in his first essay as Conservative election agent, told the Junior Conservatives on Mon- day that Mr. Herbert Gladstone had knocked the bottom out of the Aliens Bill, and that all the consid- eration was shown for the Alien to the detriment of the British workingman. This is the type of " terminological inexactitude " which calls for a short .and more pithy description. Mr. Gladstone slackened the rigours of the Aliens Bill because it was proving itself to be an instrument whereby the right of asylum in this country for the prosecuted foreign political refugee was denied. It has always been our boast that the persecuted and oppressed of all nations could find protection and safety in free England. As the Act stood it was causing Russian and other refugees of blameless character to be shipped back to torturo and death solely because they had not a certain sum of money in their pockets. This is not what the British workingman desires, and we think he will he content to know that the diseased and criminal alien is still forbidden to enter this country.

- - - I The usual batch of week-end cases came up at the Runcorn Sessions on Monday, before Messrs. E. Imison ' and T. D. Timmins. John Egan, Light-foot-square, Heath-road, was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Bridge-street on the evening of the 23rd ' ult. P.C. McKenna said dehindant was drunk and squabbling with his mother. He refused to go home quietly. He had previously been cautioned. Defendant and his father and mother said he had had drink, but was not drunk. The mother denied that she dragged j him home. A fine of ss. was imposed.—Michael Morris Rowe, a tramp, was charged with having been drunk at Halton on Sunday. P.C. Whalley said prisoner had a crowd of men around him and was singing "rho farmer's boy." He used filthy language to witness and threatened to knock his head off if he interfered witn him. He refused to go away and when arrested behaved like a madman and kicked and struck right and left. Super- intendent Ennion said prisoner was drunk when brought to the Police Station. Thar() were previousconvictions and prisoner was committed to gaol for a month.

URBAN COUNCIL ELECTIONS. Po for the Urban Council of Runcorn took place on Saturday from noon to eight o'clock in the evening. There were contests in four wards. The candidates were : Mersey Ward, Messrs. J. J. Shaw and R. H. Pringle: Newtown Ward, Messrs. J. Wilson and W. Shaw, jun.; Heath Ward, Mess's. W. Handley and G. H. Grounds; Bridgewater Ward, Messrs. G. Hewitt and G. W. Littler. Considerable interest was taken in the election, and quite lively scenes were witnessed in some of the wards. In the Mersey Ward a hundred votes were registered before one o'clock. The result of the poll was declared from the stations about half- past eight in the Mersey, Heath and Newtown Wards and nine o'clock in the Bridgewater Ward as follows : Mersey Ward. Pringle Shaw, J. An enjoyable and successfal concert was held in the Ellesmere-street Mission room on Saturday evening, presided over by Mr. J. W. Hayward J.P. Songs were rendered by Miss L. Plinston, Miss E. Teylor and Mr. 11. Plumpton, and vio!in selections by Mr. L. E. Wood. The humorous element was provided in a couple of dialogues entitled" An important omission" and "April Fools," ably given by Mr. Hedley H. Taylor and party. Mr. R. Haigh and Mr. Lomas dis- charged the duties of accompanists. Hearty votes of thanks to the chairman and artistes brought the gathering to a close. The proceeds were in aid of the funds of the sewing class which is making prepara- tions for the forthcoming bazaar.
