Ancient Order 0! A meeting of the Past and Present Officers Society in connection with the Ancient Order of Foresters was held at the Masons' Arms, Mill-street, on Monday evening. Bro. Peter Peacock, D.C.R., president, was in the chair, and was suppirted by the vice-president, Bro. W. Hipkiss, P.D.C.R., and a good number of members.—The committee appointed at the last meeting to draw up the rules, presented their report and it was unanimously carried. -During the evening Bro. G. ldaybury, P.D.C.R., read a paper on the pro- ceedings of the Annual National Conference held at Southampton, on Friday, March 23.-1 n interesting discussion took place on, Bro. Maybury's paper in which Bros. Peacock, D.C.R., Hipkiss, P.D.C.R., Chrirnes, P.D.C.R., Thornley, P.D.C.R., and L. Davies, district secretary, took part. A vote of thanks to Bro. Maybury brought the proceedings to a close.

The concluding popular penny concert of the season was given on Saturday evening in the Bold- street Wesleyan Schoolroom, when there was a large audience The first part of the programme consisted of a cantata entitled ' Sherwood's Queen," by Mr. B. Wadsworth's party, and proved highly successful, all the performers acquitting themselves in an admirable manner. The second part opened with a humorous song by Mr. J. Isherwood, for which he was warmly , applauded. Songs were given in excellent style by the Misses Leicester and Hipkiss, and a well rendered duet by Mr. and Mrs. Hannan was heartily appreciated. div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
ADULTERATED MILK.

At the \Warrington Police Court, on Monday, May Brierley. Knutsford-roal, was summoned for selling milk which was adulterated by the addition of ten per cent, of water.—lnspector Flood stated that on the 18th February be took a sample of milk at the defendant's shop and submitted it to the public analyst. It was found to contain only 8.111 of the non-fatty solids, whereas samples taken at the barn from which the defendant was supplied and from the farmer's cart, con- tained an average of 8.9 non-fatty solids.—ln answer to Mr. Steel, witness said he bad constantly taken samples of milk from the defendant's shop, and the sample in question was the first one about which there was any- thing wrong.—Defendant denied having added water to the milk. She sOld it exactly as she received it.—Mr. Steel having addressed tho magistrates, a fine of 10s. was inflicted. TIM WARRINGTON BURNING TRAGEDY. At the Warrington Police Court, on Monday, Thomas Mitchell, son of a Ship-yard lodging-house keeper, was again brought before the magistrates. Mitchell was arrested ostang to the dying deposition of a widow named Susatuth Flavell,who accused him of having set her on fire on March 24th,1n a lodging-house—The Chief Constable explained that the woman accused Mitchell of having set her (mike. She was suffering greatly at the time and there were grave donbts as to the truth of her statement. This was borne out by the woman admitting to the Rev. W. Bracecamp, vicar of St. Paul's, whom she knew very well, that her statement was false, and :laying that she set herself on fire while smoking— The evidence of Mr. Bracecamp was put before the jury at the Coroner's inquest, with the result that Mitchell was exonerated, and he was allowed out on bail. There was no stain or suspicion against him so far as his case was concerned, and therefore he would not offer any evidence against the prisoner.—Mitchell was then dis- charged.

div.head: FALL THROUGII A ROOF.
div.p: FALL THROUGII A ROOF.

Margaret O'Malley, a stranger, who appeared in the dock at the Borough Police Court on Tuesday, with her head wrapped in bandages, was charged with being found on the enclosed premises of the British Work- man Cocoa-rooms,Bridge-street,early that morning, for an unlawful purpose.—Superintendent Monaghan said that shortly After midnight the manager heard voices at the rear of his prernises,and a ladder was reared against the wall. Immediately afterwards a crash of glass was heard, and on going into the lavatory prisoner was found on the floor blee2ling from wounds on the head, baying fallen through a glass roof--s distance of nine feet. A man was with her, but she refused to divulge anything.—Prisoner was remanded for a week. ASSAULT ON A WORKHOUSE INMATE. - •• - • - • - ^

..„ James Hopkins, who was described by the Chief Con- stable of Warrington as one of the worst characters in the neighbourhood, was sent to goal at the Warrington Police Court on Wednesday, for two months for assault- ing a Warrington Workhouue inmate named Bolton. The latter stated that Hopkins came into the work- house that morning in a drunken condition, and in con- sequence of some remarks Hopkins struck him several times in the face knocking him to the floor. The Chief Constable said Hopkins had been before the bench thirty- flee times. He was a burden on the ratepayers either in gaol or in the workhouse. CARTER'S TtiFFT FROM A BREWERY. At the Warrington Police Court, on Weddesday, Mathew Doming, carter, 110, Higher Parr-street, St. Helens, was charged with stealing a brass tap and union value Os. Gd. from Messrs. Peter Walker and Son's brewery. Dallam-lane Warrington. Prisoner was em- ployed by Mr.. Swift, licensee of the Fornacemen's Arms, as a carter' and on the 31st ult. he was sent for a load of broken bottle glass from Messrs. Walker's premises. Mist in the back office he torrethe tap and union. On arrival at St. Helens he was questioned by Mr.' Swift with regard to some corn, and a search of a box at the back of the lorry revealed the brass articles. The prisoner failed to give a satisfactory account of the brass and bolted, but was captured and given into custody. The magistrates seot him to gaol for two months. Mr. Swift was complimented for his action in the matter.
In Anglesey there Fe thirty-eight pnrishes, together containing a population or 10,000 people, which have not a single public-house in them. This is considered to be a record.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
RUGBY FOOTBALL.
By " Ovalist "

Warrington are in the semi-final —or rather one of the semi-finals is in Warrington. which is inteiesting j but not quite the same thing:rife Northam Union Com- mittee on Mond, decided that the semi-final between Broughton Rangers or Salford and Keighley should bs played at Warrington, and though the match is not likely to produce a Titanic struggle' still it should Attract a considerable crowd. Keighley have been here before, notably a year ago when they drew with Warrington in a cup tie hut lost the relay at Keighley.

Warrington just managed to win at Rochdale on Saturday by the, only try scored in the game. Thus for the third time this seas in they took full points from the Hornets. A more uninteresting match could hardly have been played and throughout the eighty minutes there was not a solitary _sparkling incident Even the. try which won the match was a nondescript, fluky sort of affair, which required little skill to obtain and provided nothing to enthuse about. Warrington were, though practically at full strength, nearly as bad as the Hornets and did not deserve more than one point. They played very lackadaisical football throughout and if the forwards had not been about as heavy again as the home lot, the Hornets might have snatched a vic- tory by sheer perseverance. Perhaps the fact that the team was unattended by a committeeman on Saturday had something to do with the easygoing style of play. It makes a lot of difference .to a paid footballer when the official eye is upon him.

There was practically no breeze on Saturday, but curiously enough both sides attacked persistently from the town end. Tho Hornets had all the play up to half-time, and Warrington only crossed the centre line about three times. Yet it was clear that they could do better if they wished and there was not much danger from the Hornets unless somebody made a bad slip. They kept attacking but were easily repulsed. A good deal depended on Berry at times and he pro- bably had the busiest afternoon he has had since he played full back ;only his steadiness once or twice pre- vented the Hornets from crossing the line.

During the interval the Warrington, men had a confab with the sponge-bearer and bag-carrier-in- chief who presumably represented the committee, and on resuming there was a more businesslike air about the men. The forwards buckled to and Rochdale had

_ to retire permanently to their own quarter. Several good passing movements on the Warrington side nearly succeeded, but neither Fish nor Taylor Ntere quite fast enough to put on the finishing touch. Threequarter time at rived before any score came, and then it was through Blincow hampering Rigg and causing the veteran full-back to make his first mis- take. The two men missed the ball and Hockenhall dribbled to the line, where he crossed the ball to Fish who was able to touch down unopppsed. The home team was unfortunate to have such a try against them, and a little temper was shown in the concluding stages. Somebody laid Swift low, and then he was caught retaliating with a straight right and ordered into retirement by the referee. Warringtoa stood their ground well with a man short and were near scoring again before the close.

cannot honeitly award praise to many of the Warrington men. Derry was in fine form, and some good work was done by Isherwood, bit the rest of the team seemed content to hold the Hornets cheap. The halves had possession ahnosi constantly but were slow in getting the ball away, while Dickinson fre- quently neld too long in the centre. Blincosv played a fine game for Rochdale, and wAs well suppirted by Rigg and Baxter, but the team generally was no match' for the Warrington men v.rien it came to attacking.

To-day IVarrington are at home to Hull, and expectations of a good match shouid be realised. Hull play as open a game as at in the Union and on their last visit to Warrington there was some very free scoring in a splendidly cmtested match. Warring- ton eventually won by 13 points to 11 points, and I should not be surprised to see a similar display to- day. Since the New Year Hull have improved very much and with such men as Parry, Freear, Burehell and Taylor in the back division are not to be lightly esteemed. They beat Warrington pretty comfortably at Hull, but the tables should be turned to-day if Warrington show anything like the determina- tion one expects from them at Wildersoool. They will have to play a far different game from that of [ last week however.

There' are only two clianges from the team which won at Rochdale, Knight displacing Berry and Harmer coming in for Swift. Warrington people will svmpathise with the young Warrington full-back, Berry, in the loss of his father this week. The selected tenm is as follows : Knight, full back ; Fish, Jsherwood, Dickenson and Taylor, three- quarters ; Lees and Hockenball, half-backs, Preston, Boardman, Heath, Thomas, Shugars, Harmer, Belton and Jolley, forwards.

The" A " team has an inportant Combination match at Oldham and a big effort mill made to win. Hallam returns to the side, which is a strong one,viz. : Hallam, fall back ; Jordan, Brooks, Cartwright and Kenyon, threequarters ; Lambert and Lloyd, half backs ; Bradshaw, Morrison, Hewitt, Ashton and Forster forwards, One point will secure the cham- pionship, which in any Case ought to be safe seeing that St. Helens" A " have to come to win yet.

There has been a rare struggle for supremacy between Broughton Rangers and Salford for entry into the semi-final, and a third meeting at Wigan this (Friday)..evenin7 at 5.30 is necessary to settle the matter. The Rangers ought to have nipde themselves secure at Broughton on Wednesday, but some unaccountable fumbling by Wilson certainly lost their winning chances. The other re-play at Halifax between the home team and Bradford on Tuesday pro- duced a surprise, for Bradford beat their famous opponents in decisive fashion for the first time lin a cup-tie. They will now meet and probably can- quer Batley 'at Huddersfield. I rather fancy the Bradford men's chances for the Cup seeing that they have not got Warringtou to fear this time. The last two years has seen them twice upset in the semi-final by a" wire "entanglement.

Warrington Club members will be interested and none too pleased—to learn that they will have to pay to witness the semi-final at Wilderapsol on the 14th. The Northern Union rules are imperative on this matter and all members will have to pay Is. to enter the ground. They should not begrudge this seeing that Warrington has been honoured for the first time with a semi-final match, and moreover the com- mittee are arranging special seating accommodation for all members inside the rails and round the ground. The Club only gets 10 per cent of the takings, and stands to make no profit on the match. An effort is being made to get the postponed Hunslet match arranged for the following Saturday, the 21st, when both Clubs have a vacant date.
I have been permitted to see the sample medals for the Works Competitiop winners and runners-up. The design and quality of both are excellent and the medals are well worth striving for.

div.head: Hockey.
div.p: Hockey.
On Saturday last the Stockton Heath club completed a successful season when they visited. Ilebington, the result of the match wus a draw, both sides scoring two goals.

The first half was evenly contested, but the home side crossed over leading 1-0, and when a second was added after a few minutes play in the second half, things looked black for the visitors. From this point till the end however Stockton Heath played up, and eventually managed to draw level, R. Pierpoint and W. H. Banks scoring the goals. For Stockton Heath the defence played a fine game, and the famous Bebington wing, Draper and F. B. Peel, were given little chance to shine.
The second eleven visited Frodsham, and after a game in which they ont-played the home side at all points, ran out winners by 3 —l. The goals were scored by T. Day 2, H. Owen 1.

Stockton Heath on Saturday secured a handsome victory at the exams() of New Brighton after a hard game. For the florae team Sampson at full back 'played a fine game his kicking and fielding being excellent. The threequarter line as a whole combined well although the centres were inclined to be rather selfish when a pass out to the wings would have gained ground. E. G. Holden who made A reappear- ance after several weeks absence played a sound game and G. Langley also did well. The half backs, H. Davenport and C. Hawthorne played a fine game and made plenty of openings, Hawthorne in particalar got the ball away from the scrums in fine style, The forwards played an excellent game and beat the heavier New Brighton eight for possession while not inferior in the loose. W. Smith, A. Cooke, K. Gibbs, and D. Skelton all did well and J. Daintith in the open was very useful._

div.head: Bowling.
div.p: Bowling.

Mr. A. 11. Crosfleld, M.P., has long been known as an ardent supporter of the summer sport and a high honour has been conferred upon him by his election as president of the Lancashire and Cheshire County Bowling Asso- ciation. This is one of the most important bowling organizations in the connty and Mr. Crostield is to be congratulated upon his election Whilst the association is also to be complimented upon having selected a gentleman upon whom to confer their highest honour, who will take a keen interest in the well being of the body.

It was interesting to hear that when Mr. Manning suggested the holding of the concerts nearly everyone. prophesied failure. The direct contrary, however, has been the case, the concerts having been ran for twenty-five consecutive weeks. Moreover, the bulk of the .talent has been voluntary. A committee of men connected with Bold-street and who were in sympathy with the sclienae and in touch with musical people, managed the arrangements, and this fact Mr. Manning considers is to a great extent the secret of success. The plan was that each member of the committee should in turn be responsible for a concert, and it worked admirably. Mr. E. Plinston has acted as secretary and done splendid work, as have also Mr. Frank Hickman, Mr. Tom Brough, and Mr. T. Stringer (treasurer). It is gratifying to know that with such small prices of admission, no financial loss has been experenced, and this should 'encourage the workers to .greater efforts in the future. The concerts will be resumed in October, but Mr. Manning is hoping to go a step further during the winter and provide a men's institute, to be open every night of the week. We wish the scheme every succegs.

Ruby is chemically composed of alumiria, or oxide of aluminium, together with a minute proportion of chromium, which gives the charactristic, colour. The problem to be faced in making artificial rubies is to melt snob a mixture and allow it to solidify into a crystal free from flaws and large bubbles. To melt it in any ordinary way, as, for instance, by directing an oxy-hydrogen blowpipe on to a lump of the material, is quite useless, since an opaque mass full of cracks is all that results. M. Verneuil has found, however, that if the mass is gradually built up by the successive addition of ; Powdered material, while it is _kept melted by • the blowpipe flame, a large and transparent cryst&l can be obtained. He ingeniously effects this by making the gases of the blowpipe convey this powder on to the mass while they keep it hot. The blowpipe is directed downwards, and the current of powder is fed into it through a concentric tube, which is continually tapped, so as to ensure a constant supply. THE SLEEP OF PLANTS. That sleep at regular intervals and for certain periods is necessary to the well-being of animals, man included, we all know. That Plants, in their turn, need periods of repose, although equally appreciated by the botani,c, is an item of nature knowledge in possession only of a .few, perhaps, ‘ ' says Cassell's Popular Science." it does not I hold outside scientific circles. This position is tie outcome, in a great measure, of regarding animal and vegetable kingdoms as related, if at all, only in a minor degree, or. rather, of looking upon them as things apart -and irre- trievably separated. Plants must sleep, as well as animals. and if the sleep of the former has in i vim° respects rather a different significance than it has in the latter. yet the two have also many points of resemblqice, or at least of , analogy. The owner of a garden or grounds ; well stocked with plants, if he is ,at all obser- ; cant. cann3t but have been charmed with the bright and open-faced appearance of everything !on a clear morning, especially if it has rained over night or a heavy dew is lying on the plants. The cheerful appearanci, of everything may be maintained throughout the day; but if the observer lingers long after sundown, and the i dew begins to fall. he is almost certain to he struck with the altered a,spect •of something ho I may have been looking at during the day. div.head: WIRE THAT IS INVISIBLE.
div.p: WIRE THAT IS INVISIBLE.

Invisible -platinum wire is stated to have been drain by the late Henry 1. Read a third of a century ago. Several yards were made, in • lengths of aft. or less, and when wound Upon a white card it could be felt, but ordinarily could not be seen, although its shadow was visible. The wire was drawn through •as fine a hole as ?Quid be conveniently drilled. When the plati- num was reduced to this size, it was coated with silver, and again drawn through the die. This was repeated as many times as necessary, ' when the silver was dissolved away, leaving the . fine platinum wire. The product was intended . for the cross-threads of cptical instruments. The ' animal hairs employed , were affected by damp- . aces, but the brightness of the metal proved an sven more serious disadvantage, so it never : same into use. Spiders' web is now used.

ITHE PROBLEM OF LAKE TANGANYIKA. Lake Tanganyika in East -Central Africa is i notable as the longest freshwater lake in the ' world. It is still more remarkable as the habitat of two' species of Mediisa. For these organisms, otherwise known as jelly fish, are only known elsewhere as inhabitants of salt water. To ac- count for this curious occurrence of marine forms in 'a fresh water lake, Mr. J. E. Moore has sug- gested that Lake Tanganyika represents an old urassic farm of the sea. In other words, the sea iii Jurassic times extended into Central Africa, and when it retired a lake was left. The marine element in its fauna would be the result of its former connection with the ocean. Dr. Calman and Mr. Boulengen, however, adopt a I somewhat different view. They . consider that ! the present fauna of Tanganyika is the result of long isolation. expressing itself in " diverg.nt evolution and specialisation." And in this con nection it may be noted that a marine crustacean . has been obtained in Lake Geneva at a cl4th of 130 ft.

Once again the smart little fawn coat has dome into favour for spring wear. I th,ink we should all welcome it heartily, for it certainly may be reckoned among the most useful and economical of garments, as it can be worn indiscriminately over all sorts of frocks--dressy and plain. - A very pretty example of these short, coats Is illus- trated in our sketch. The material of which it is fashioned is a fine smooth cloth, in colour a light beige, a shade something between biscuit and lawn. The coat is quite tight-fitting, with the

exceptlt,„ _ two fiords, which have a sugges- tion of striughtness about their cut. They have their edges turned in and firmly machined. and are further adorned with large handFome buttons. Above these fronts turn back two little rounded rekvers, also stitched. The back of the coat is adorned with a velvet collar of a slightly darker tone. The sleeves are of the gigot type, and have epaulette strappings at the top.

UNCLE NED. -
At school we have been studying in our history, the battle of Bosworth. It was fought between Richard 111. ot England and Henry, Earl of Richmond, who wished to take the crown from Richard.

When I reached home I thogght I would try to write a poem on that subject, which you see I _ have done. , Will you please publish it in your Children's Corner ". When teacher saw it he said it was very good, and read it aloud to all the class.
I remain your affectionate nephew, SYDNEY WILKES.
THE BATTLE OF BOSWORTH.

'Twas fatal Bosworth field That Gloucester lost that day, And many a hardy blow he dealt Amid the thickest fray. Think ye of the men were slain, In that deadly fight, Of the blood, and of the pain, It was a dreadful sight! He was brave in spirit, and strong in limb, Nor from the fight did he fly; When half his forces deserted him, His warriors heard him cry:—
" Give me my sword, Place the crown on my head! For by sunset I shall be dead!"

So said the king As to the conflict he dashed; While his bright mail and blade In the broad sunlight flashed. On the right, and on the left, from behind and before, He was surrounded by knights And they pressed him sore.
Then his last moments came, It was true what he said: lie struck his last blow, And Gloucester was dead!

JOHNNY ONIONS. It was a bitter cold day in December, and Southampton was wrapped In a damp fog. Johnny Onions came whistling down the street to keep himself warm, as he went from house to house trying tso sell his onions. When he reached a certain house in Millbrook Road, he saw A little girl sitting at the window looking sulkily out. " I should'nt look cross if I lived in a nice warm house like that," Johnny thought. He went to the door and rang the bell, a lady came an 4, asked him what he wanted. "Any onionsorery cheap, the last this winter," asked the boy. 'Not to-day, thank you," the lady answered." "Very cheap ma'am," and as the boy spoke he shivered with the cold. The lady svv how cold he was, and asked him if he would Tike a cup of cocoa. He flushed with pleasure, and said he would. The lady (whose name was Mrs. Carr) took him into a warm kitchen, and made him a hot cup of cocoa.' She then called her little daughter to go to the boy and ask him if he would like something to eat. Hilda went as her mother told her, but very slowly, for she was still sulky beeause she could not go for a walk, but when she saw the poor boy enjoying his warm drink she was ashamed that she should grumble when she had every- thing she wauted. So she went up to him and said, "Oh, Johnor Onions, I hope you are enjoy- ing your cocoa, for you look so cold." "Thank you, Miss, I like it very much." Hilda was only eight years old, so she soon became friendly with the boy. "Where do you live, Johnny?" The boy's lace brightened, while he answered, "I am going home to-morrow in a steamer which is called "Hilda," and I shall see my mother, too." ‘"lam

THE SQUIRREL ROBBED. One bright autumn day . A squirrel said, "As the nuts are beginning to to Jail, I'd better get in my winter store If I hope to have any at all."
Then quick with his little nimble feet, And his sharpness of white little teeth, He gathered and dropped them One by one to the ground beneath.
He soon had a pile as large as himself, And thought "what a hole I must dig!" When just one more caught his squirrel eye Far up on the top-most twig.
Then down he ran, but the nuts were gone, Not one was left for his winter's store, And he angrily curled his bushy tail, And snapped his teeth till his jaws were sore.
" I wish I could find the thief," said he, "I'd give him a nut to crack'; Ha, ha, laughed the boy from behind the tree As he ran with the nuts on his back. from your loving niece, LAURIE WOODS.

Dear Uncle Ned, I write to let you know how pleased I was to see my name in the paper. lam glad to be a member of the Children's Corner League, and I hope you will get a lot more members. I have got a list of 24 ne,w members, so will you for- ward me a Form, for which I enclose a stamped envelope. lam sending you a little story called OBEYING ORDERS. A farmer had a tine crop which he did not want the huntsmen to ride over, so he hired a lad to keep the gate shut. The horsemen came along and told him to open the gate. He refused.' They offered him money, but he would not take it. Then one of them said, "My boy, lam the Duke of Wellington, and I command you to open the gate." The boy took off his cap and said, "I am sure the Duke ot Wellington would not wish me to disobey orders. I must keep this gate shut. No one can pass through without my master's permission." The Duke raised his hat and replied, "Quite right my lad, I honour the man or boy who can neither be bribed nor frightened into wrong-deing. I remain, your loving niece. LIZZIE RICHARDSON.

HELPER'S MOTTO.
A little thing—a sunny smile, a loving word at
morn, And all day long the sun shone on, The cares of life were made more light, And sweeter hopes were born.
A little thing—a hasty word, a cruel frown at morn, And aching hearts went on theit way, And toiled throughout the dreary day, Disheartened, sad, and lorn. From your niece, VIOLET CUMMING.

div.head: Tide of Traffic.
div.p: The Tide of Traffic.

Given a sunny afternoon and dry roads, the Baturday cyclist does not appear to be deterred from the enjoyment of his pastime by such a trifle aS the congestion of the main roads, due to motor cars and cycles, motor busses and electric trams. This was evidenced the other Saturday on the Great North ltoad, when swarms of outward bound wheelmen accommodated themselves to the swift onrush of motor traffic, and made light of the March dust raised by the larger cars. 'Returning along the same stretch of road an hour or so later, little traffic was eneountved, proving that the rush colmtrrwards occurs mostly between 3 and 4.30 Ladies, or nerv.uus riders, who dislike crowds may therefore avoid discomfort by timing their start either before or after the " rush " hours, pre- feEably on the earlier side, so that they may regain home before the turn in the tide of traffic.

div.head: Do Fewer Ladies Cycle?
div.p: Do Fewer Ladies Cycle?

The übiquitous lady cyclist "is a term that has ceased to be accurate—says the writer of a ladies' section. In large cities the falling off is ascribed to the growth of -motor traffic, but it is admitted that in the cOuntily and at the seaside little decline is observable. Even during the winter months the fashionable lady residents at Tunbridge Wells, for example, are to be seen any fine day making use of their wheels on shopping visits •to the Pantiles... Nor can • the present fashion of the trimmed, shaped skirt be held responsible for feminine abstention, from the saddle; for, t since the days whefi ladies' raiment got wound up in the gear wheels of sociable tricycles, there has never been a time when a specially made cycling skirt was not a necessary equipment for safe and comfortable riding. iliersorurl observation leads this writer to the conclusion that it ls not correct to suppose that . fewer ladies cycle. The facts are rather in the other direction, and this is confirmed by the numbers of ladies' cycles still sold bY lead- ing manufacturers.

Frequent raids by the police seem to have little effect in lessening the number of enstaunos who make the Manchester brickcrofts their sleeping Piece. A further batch of 22 appeared before the magistrates on Tuesday. The Home Office has authorised governors of convict prisons to permtt Jewish prisoners to be exempt frrm labour during the Passover, commencing at noon on the 9th inst.

div.head: Warrington Win at Rochdale,
div.p: Warrington Win at Rochdale,

On Saturday, Warrington took to Rochdale one of the strongest teams they have been able to get togetker this year. Hookenhall, Dickenson, and Boardman all returned to the side after recent injuries. The hp:nesters were also well representeil, Schofield being<the principal absentee. Eine weather favoured the fixture, but there would not be more than 2,500 spectators. Teams and officials :

Rochdale Horne/ts.—Rigg (captain), back ; Gibson, Devitt, Blincow' and Evans, three-quarter backs ; Baxter and Kiley, half backs ; Crabtree, Richardson, Ashton, Hurst, Shaw, Hyde, Liley, and Hallworth, forwards. ilarrington—Berry, back; Fish, Isherwood, Dicken- son, and Taylor, three-quarter backs; Hockenball and Lees, half backs ; Preston, Boardman, Swift. Thomas, Jolley, Shunirs,yeath, and Morrison, forwards. . _ .

Reree, Mr. F. Kennedy, Broughton. Touch judges : Messrs. Platt, Swinton, and W. Mainwaring, Salford. Rigg started the game and the home forwards rushed the ball over tbe line right away. Fish having to send it dead. A burst by the Warrington forwards was saved by Kiley, and eventually the Hornets invaded close to the line, where Blincow and Gibson had bard luck. Evans was conspicuous with a brilliant piece of play, and the Warrington men had their work cut out to keep their line intact. Fish received and dashed down the field, but finally Hurst saved in smart style. The Hornets transferred play to the Warrington half, and play ruled close to the line, Berry twice saving very pluckily. Fish and Isherwood relieved, but the Hornets continued to have the best of the game up to half-time, which arrived with no score. Preston re-started and l3lincow and Rigg were early called upon to defend. The Warrington men showed rather more determination and several passing move- ments nearly resulted in the line being crossed. Once, Dickenson rushed over after following up a kick, but was called back. The Hornets tried hard to cldar their lines but were beaten for possession. About three- quarter time the only score of the match came. Blincow and Rigg were undecided about fielding a lofty punt, when Hockenhall nipped between them and getting the ball to his toes near the line he crossed to Fish who recorded a simple try near the corner. Preston tailed at goal.' The Hornets played with considerable spirit after this and some temper was shown with the result that Swift (Warrington) was sent off. Though a man short for the rest of the game Warrington easily held the upper hand and but for Taylor being lame would have added to the score. Final : Warrington, one try; Rocl.dale Hornets, nil.

div.head: LANCASHIRE COMBINATION.
div.p: LANCASHIRE COMBINATION.
WARRING TON "A " v. ROCHDALE "A."

Played at Warrington on Saturday. Roclpdale played against the breeze during the first stage, and were early forced to defend. A movement from Lloyd was intercepted, and Lee taking the game too near centre, the Rochdale men followed up the advantage, for Chorley kicking across to Ricbaraon, that player exhibited a rare turn of speed and scored at the corner. The Rochdale men only enjoyed their lead a few moments, for fine work by Jordan and Forster pnded in Jordan scoring. Near the interval Brooks crossed after fine passing. The Rochdale defence failed signally, and Kenyon. Brooks, and Lambert added tries the I.Varrington men leading at the interval by five tries (15 point), to Rochthle Hornets, one try (three points). In the second half Warrington were again the better side and fine play was exhibited by Cartwright, Forster, and Brooks. The passing of the backs was well timed, and tries were scored by Brooks (2) and Cart- wright, two goals being placed by Forster. Final : Warrington, two goals eight tries (28 points) ; Rochdale Hornets, one try (three points).

div.head: POETRY AND POLITICS.
div.p: POETRY AND POLITICS.
• •-• very iii.ilziress by the Rev. C H. Cook.

The last meeting for the session of the Warrington Junior Liberal Association was held at Gregory's Cafe on Monday evening, when an address was delivered by the Rev. C. Harvey Cook on " Poetry and Politics." Mr. E. Osborne presided over a fair attendance. Poetry and Politics, said Ur. Cook, would seem, to superficial judgment, miles apart. The ,paradox of I associating the mount of the muses with the science of , government was more apparent than real, but rather than being antipathetic toe-aids each other, there was the deepest mutual sympathy between the two. ' They must clear their minds of all cant about poetry, and have a clear notion of what they meant by it. It was hela by some that poetry was merely a means through words of conveying pleasurable sensual sensa- tions. Could such liltings of language be ever named poetry? Poetry was, he apprehended, creative thought —thought which clothed the impossible in fact, which brought, as it were, out of nothing, all things. Every politician ought to be, at least, if not a poet, a I companion of the poets. They wanted politieians whose sojourn with the poets so saturated and penetrated their individualities that the scienee I of government might become actualized poetry. l James Russell Lowell was one of America's finest noets of politics, and to his muse all men surely who had any I faith at all in progress and betterment, whether Con- I servative, Liberal, or Labour, responded. In some of I his lines they caught a glimpse of more th:m national I poetry. Byron's genius was a peculiar combination, his ) welding of poetry and politics arising from two very I opposite sourcei. of inspiration; his -political poetry was y largely the outcome of two conflicting Byrons in one Byron. He was an English peer, tqrned out by a pro- cess of mental dovelopment into a democrat. but forced more by circumstances into that position—a man whose sympathies were wider than his class. How Byronic , were the lines :

The army like a lion from its den, Martha forth with nerve and sinew bent to slay, A human hydra issuing from its fen, To breathe distruction on its winding way. Evan that was poetry and politics. Burns' muse would have been no small means in bringing to account 'man's highest dreams with Heaven's decree.' " Tbe tree of liberty" was a political poem which every politician ought to be made to learn by heart. It was the poetry of the science of government expressed in lyric strains. Plato had left it on record that it was well fora state _.

when its statesmen were philosophers. With such a high authority one would not even dare to dispute, but simply suggest that it wore well for a State if its statesmen were poet-philosophers. Walt Whitman was not kno,!n as. his muse deserved to be known; per-

chance it was becawe of the heterodoxy of his lierary and poetic style. So many people had an idea that poetry must be rhyme that they could not read with any real intellectual enjoyment.ln poems one line might contain lG words, and the next line eight, and tho words could not be made to jingle. In consequence, many folk would not take the intellectual trouble to grasp the poetry, because it vras not presented in rhyme form. (Applause.) The voices of the poets needed to be needed as well as the voices of the doctrinaires if the science of govern- ment was to be codified. (Applause.) An interesting discussion followed, and Mr. Cook wra heartily thanked for his paper.

LETTERS TO THE EDITOR.
NOTICE TO CORRESPONDENTS. Authors of letters intended for publication must in all cases send their names and addresses to the Editor as a guarantee of good faith.

"The New Factor in British Politics." Sir, I wish to correct an error in vow report of the weekly meeting of the Junior Liberals held on Monday the 25th ult. It is stated: "Mr. Matthews in replying disagreed with M.r.'o%borne's Vi9W4 that Socialists were atheists, and hoped Mr. Osborne would rid himself completely of that idea." I have never held that "Socialists were Atheists." What I did say was, that it was unfortunate that an attempt was being made by the Editor of the "Clarion." to drag Socialism at the heels of atheism—an entirely different thing. I contended that such behaviour was a serious menace to the progress of the movement. I am a Socialist; but I am not an atheist.— Yours truly, EDMUND OSTIORNE. 29, Lovely-lane, Warrington. 2nd April, 1906.

div.head: Association Football.
div.p: Association Football.

Sir,—Why is there not a Warrington Association Football Club? Why? That question has been asked of many people on many occasions, hut the answer has not been 'forthcoming. Prompted by the excellent exposition of the game on Saturday last, the writer is anxious to ascertain, if possible what are the stumbling blocks, if any, to the formation of a club for Warring- ton. and he would be obliged if you, Sir, would allow a little of your space to be used for that purpose. The President of the Warrington District Association in responding to a toast at the dinner on Saturday is reported to have said that." It was owing to the efforts of the Executive Committee in getting the game to such a successful condition." Is the game in a success- ful condition? Is the Executive Committee respon- sible for such condition? One of the speakers, the first chairman of the Association, stated that, " Association Football in Warrington had not made the progress it ought to have done." Well, who is responsible for that? Ido not wish to press home any point either for or against any members of the Executive Committee. Doubtless there are many reasons why the game has not flourished and it is purely in the interests of the game believing as I do that the time is now ripe fora flourish- ing team to be established, that I address you. I hope that there will he an expression of opinion from those who take art interest in Association Football and its -charms,—Yours etc.
FULL-BACK.

div.head: Religious Instruction.—Reply to Canon
div.p: Religious Instruction.—Reply to Canon
Stevenson.

Sir,—Shades of Homer ! Has Caon Stevensen been •caught napping ? or am o visions about ? He is reported to have told the people at Hamilton-street Schools in a recent speech that Mr. Matthews had quoted from an .old Blue Book. I gave the date 1902. Is that old ? I make Canon Stevenson a present of every mistake he can find, either in the Blue Book or my letter. I even go further, and admit for the sake of argument that the 'Government contributions to buildings in Warrington and the county generally are comparatively poor, and scarcely worth notice. Even then my argument has not been touched. Nor does Canon Stevenson's long and intimate knowledge of Warrington and its schools affect the argument either. It is still true that education is a public charge ; that school buildings have been in part a public charge, and now for the future are likely to be completely so ; and that this being so, citizen rights must be respected. They would be violated by any specific treatment to Denominationalists. Again, Canon Stevenson answers my plea for frank- ness on the part of the clergy, by the counter-assertion that he has always stood for fair play." That is so : but Canon Stevenson's " fair play ' means right of entry for all denominations in public elementary schools. Free Churchmen repudiate the principle, nor can they have it thrust upon them by the well-meaning and even engaging despotism of a most genial clergy- man like Canon Stevenson. _ _

May I direct public attention to a very silly remark that has often been made in this education controversy? Imagine, say Denominationalists, a Baptist or Wes- leyan as the headteacher of a Roman Catholic school! or,a Roman Catholic as the head of a Wesleyan school? I can't imagine any such thing. Under direct public control, State schools will ultimately cease to be *known by and thought of as Roman Catholic, Anglican, or Nonconformist. What is more, and what is better still, the atmosphere of the publicly-controlled school, divorced from so-called religious teaching, will be inimical neither to the faith of the R.C. nor any other denominationalist, while at the same time it wit offer to the ambitious teacher desirous of excelling in his profession, the possibility of securing 9. headship, with- out any inquiries being made, except as to his fitness and the value of his intelle,tual endowments.

May I thank you, sir, for the courtesy you have •extended to me in your columns and the very generous kindness of those who have had to take exception to what I have written ? I would ask the publie not to be led away, however, by the bogey of secularism. What is called secularism is certainly rife in our day; perhaps it has never been more rife than at present. But. like all negations, it carries with it the germs of its own decay. In my intercourse with young men, I have found that secularism has invariably been begotten of the creeds which they have learnt at school.lt is not the Living Christ they attack, but the " creeds, "which are supposed to explain Him and His teachings. Banish these from the schools; leave the Churches to teach their own form of religion ; gather in the children and train them in love, wisdom, and goodness, and to me, at least, the future godliness of our country seems assured.— "Tours, &c.,

div.head: JOHN FRANCIS 3IATTHEWS. The Roman Position in the Education
div.p: JOHN FRANCIS 3IATTHEWS. The Roman Position in the Education
Controversy.

Sir,—The attitude of our Roman Catholic friends in the Education controversy necessarily arouses keen interest. it is certainly a curious comment on their claims to be the friends of religious liberty that they should ask for privileges for themselves from which 'others are to be excluded. The present crisis gave them an opportunity of taking a course that would have given them all that they required without doing any ill-turn to their neighbours. They had the chance of identifying themselves with an unselfish national policy on the lines of equal liberty for all. They have however in the :narrowest spirit, chosen to take the line of liberty for themselves while exhibiting the disposition to deprive Churchmen if they can of the like advantage. Naturally members of the Church of England are not going to allow such an act of opeu hostility to pass without criticism,while they may very well disclaim all responsi- bility for the controversy that has been raised. Of .course we claim the right to examine the title of the Church of Rome to a position of ascendency in this country;. we claim also the right to examine her .claim to be regarded as a friend of religious liberty ; and also as a minor issue we claim to discuss the littitude of a body with such pretensions to liberty -towards the Nationalist movement in Ireland as one aspect of her attitude towards nationalities generally. On this latter topic I may say that I cannot help feel- ing that history is not a very strong point with those of our Nationalist friends who are looking to the Church of Rome for sympathy in their aspirations. Have they not overlooked the fact, mentioned in most of the school histories, that Pope Alexander III.; -actually gave Ireland to the English Sovereign, Henry 11., and it is from his reign, I suppose, that we must , date the beginning of that ascendency which our Nationalist friends now groan under. The Pope, in the good old days, used to give these little 'things away, much in the way that Don Quixote promised dukedoms, principalities &c., to his squire, Sancho Panza. Did , not the same Pope also give away England itself to the French King Philip Augustus in the reign of King John as he also gave away the Kingdom of Portugal to Count de Bologna. So that after all the Pope himself is responsible for the English ascendency in Ireland, just as he is also responsible for the system of penal laws by which that ascendency was enforced, a system that is more distinctly asso- ciated with Papal authority than with any other ! government either here or on the Continent. So much J for the claims of the Church of Rome as a friend of religious liberty. The truth is that the Roman system is one that does not admit of a place being found for what is ordinarily understood by religions liberty. Given an infallible authority clothed with secular or temporal , authority to enforce its sentences, and such a thing as religious liberty becomes an impossibility. And as an up-to-date illustration of this I may inform your readers that on Thursday next (Maundy Thursday) there will be, or used to be recited in some of the Roman Churches the famous bull In Coma Domini, which Con- sists of a long series of imprecations against all Pro- , testations, Princes, Parliaments and people, whom it ; anathematizes as heretics, and, as heretics incapable by the papal law, not only of enjoying civil powers and rights, but as liable to temporal penalties and even to death. I believe the formality of the publication of this bull, which owed its origin mainly to Pius V. and was subsequently renewed by twenty different Popes, is now omitted at Rome but that it ' is implicitly in vigour in all its extensions " was avowed by Cardinal Ersklue in 1793. In the light of all this it is curious to find our Roman Catholic friends desirous of allying themselves with the Free Churchmen with a view to squeezing Churchmen. It is however by no raeans the first time in history that the Roman Catholics have sought to make common cause with the political dissenters. They have a common ground of sympathy in the novelty of teaching which may be charged upon both. By the bye I see it was said from the pulpit of St. Mary's, Butter- market, the other Sunday that Warrington Parish Church was built for that " Holy Sacrifice of the Mass which Churchmen hold to be a blasphemous fable and I a dangerous deceit." Indeed ! I was not aware of this. , would just like to remind the preacher that the Si.crifice of the Mass as be understands it, did not exist

in his own Church as an Article of Faith when the Parish Church was founded. What is called the Mass was only changed into what it is now in the Roman Church at the beginning of the 13th century when the newly devised doctrine of Transubstantiation was decreed as an Article of Faith for the first time by Innocent 111. at the ith Council of Lateran, and made necessary to salvation. It was this newly invented doctrines never heard of till some thousand years had passed over the Church's history, that made the ordin- ance of the Holy Communion an entirely different thing to what it had previously been. The word Mass by itself means nothing. It originally signified the dis- missal °ran assembly, then it came to be used for the lassembly itself; then to signify the service. Archbishop Usher in his tract on the religion of the ancient Irish, says it often meant els Liturgy,thongh the actual cele- bration was omitted. The term Mass as applied to the Holy Communion is as old as the fourth Century.— Apologizing fo: the length of this letter, lam, ecc., E. C. E. CARLETON.

div.head: WINWICK FREE CHURCH HALL
div.p: WINWICK FREE CHURCH HALL
ANNIVERSARY CELEBRATIONS

It is just twelve months since the efforts of the War- rington Free Church Council to provide a place of worship for the Nonconformists of Winwick saw their consummation in the opening of the commodious and well-appointed Free Church Hall. The building has supplied a long felt want, the services being well attended, and the experiment—for such it undoubtedly is—has up to the present been attended with success. The anniversary was celebrated on Thursday by the holdig of a special service and public meeting. The weather was beautifully fine and a large number of Warrington people were in attendance. The preacher at the service in the afternoon was the Rev. Adam Scott, of Southport, who took for his text the words : " 'Verily, verily I say unto thee, we speak that we do know and bear witness of that we have seen " (St. John 3, 11). In the course of all eloquent sermon he pointed out that when He spoke these words to Nicodemus Christ was but beginning the witness-bearing of the centuries and opening the evangel which tens of thousands would afterwards make known to men. His declaration was that of one who knew what He spoke and had seen what he proclaimed. In all the four Gospels Jesus was the chief speaker.—His own hall- mark was upon them. There was a peculiar speech in them which was unique ; there was nothing like it in all literature. It was absolutely true that" never man spake "like the Prophet of Nazareth. Nowhere was Jesus an apologist and He never said He "supposed "a thing or represented Himself as having been persuaded of the reality or truth of anything. There was not a single argument in the Gospels from Him for what we called the necessary existence of God. Christ spoke of Him as one whom lie personally and intimately knew, ,as one with whom He had lived. He never proceeded to prove that there was a hereafter. The only thing , that in his estimation was worth calling life was eternal. He spoke of Heaven as we should speak of home. Christ had never been silenced; nothing He said had ever been disproved. Many things which were once regarded as fundamentals of the Christian faith had been set aside as erroneous and certain prophesyings of religions teachers had been proved to be false, but not a- single word Christ ever uttered had been disproved. The 1 new doctrine of evolution might have disproved certain interpretations of Scripture but it did not touch one thing our Lord and Master ever said of God and man. Fictions might be fashionable but they were ephemeral. Only truth triumphed over time and lived for ever and that was the case with the sayings of Christ. It was sometimes said to-day that the Gospel was " going" but it was not. It was coming in greater and greater power. It still cleansed moral life, healed the sores of sin, emancipated men from evil passion, and elevated the soul above the worries of life. It made men men and breathed into them eternity, and all that it did because it was His Gospel who was and is the faithful and true witness. At the conclusion of his sermon, Mr. Scott said it had afforded him a peculiar pleasure to come to that service. He had heard about their united work in that place, and he rejoiced in it, and prayed God most earnestly that however fruitful the past had been their future would be still more and more for His glory and the increase of His Kingdom.

div.head: EVENING NIEErING,
div.p: THE EVENING NIEErING,

A public meeting was held in the evening when C.E. Parker presided over a good attendance. There were also present Mrs. Valentine, Mr. Ormiston and the Revs. J. Yonge, J. F. Matthews, J. S. Hughes, C. L. Stowe and W. Harvey (Earlestown). In his report Mr. Ortniston said that during the year everything had gone on very smoothly. On the build- ing and furnishing account their total liabilities were £770 6s.9d.and their total receipts under this head £5BO 15s. 61, leaving a debit balance of £289 115.38. On the working account their total receipts were £32 Hs. 58. including £26 ss. 2d. raised by collections. The expenses amounted to £l3 3s 58. so that on the first year's work- ing they had been able to bank £l9. The congregation had supported the Free Church Council in a most admirable manner. The attendance had been well main- tained throughout and that the services were appreciated was proved by the fact that the attendances were on the increase. A spirit of Nonconformity had been raised at Winwick which had heretofore been latent, and be fore- saw a great future for the course of the spread of evan- gelical truth in their midst. In conclusion, Mr. Ormeston expressed his deep gratitude to the Rev. J. F. Matthews for his work on behalf of the hall. (Applause) Mr. C. E. Parker said that so far as the debt upon the Hall was concerned the Free Church Council wished to take their part in bearing the burden, but the more that could be raised by the people at Winwick according to their abilities the easier it would be for them to obtain outside assist- ance. The Hall existed as a visible manifestation of the unity which existed amongst the Free Churches—a tangible recognition that the cardinal features of the Gospel were far more to them than the little differences which had divided them in the past. As Free Church- men they all rallied round the green hill without the city upon which the Cross was erected. It wa..4 very pleasing that the Free Churches had gathered together and built that Hall,and thereby given expression to their unity. It was only as individuals recognized the import- ance of those things which were spiritual and eternal that the nation and the people would rise to that position which their Maker intended they should occpy. No life was complete unless it had been touched with the spirit from above and he hoped the Hall would be a greAt influence for good in the neigh- bourhood. (Applause.) Mrs. Valentine said they must all remember that they had certain responsibility with regard to the Church—responsibilities for protecting and preserving its honour—and only as they recognized their duty would be the growth or downfall of the Church. (Hear, hear.) The Rev. W. Harvey, secretary of the District Free Church Council, said he hoped that at Winwick they wonld do as well in the future as in the past. They had given an object lesson to the world as to what Christian unity really meant—an object lesson which he thought at least the missionary societies should emulate. He might he wrong but he thought if they did so they would be doing much for the spread of the Kingdom of God and in the direction of the civiliza- tion of the nations of ,the world. (Applause.) The Rev. J. F. Matthews, who was heartily received, said the work would be exceedingly heavy if it were not for the willing co-operation of the voluntary preachers whose services were given gratuitously. The ministers of the different Free Churches in Warrington, he could assure them, were heartily in sympathy with the work at Winwick and he hoped they would shortly have practical evidence of this by the holding of a collection throughout the Churches to help forward 'the funds of the Hall. He looked forward to the time when they would have a paid minister of their own and he firmly believed that until they had some minister who would look up and visit the people the Hall would not really be the centre of usefulness and good which it ought to be. He also urged the great necessity for the establishment of a Holiday school. He was not oblivious to the difficulties of the neighbourhood. They had had to face those difficulties in the past, and they would face them again, and he hoped that before long they would have a flourishing Sunday school connected with the Hall. I (Applause). Mr. Matthews announced that the Hall WAS to be registered for the celebration of marriages. ; (Applause). The Rev. J. S. Hughes, referring to the accounts, said he had not found a place of worship of a similar size to that building which had been so economically worked. He hoped that as time went on the congregation would grow more vigorous and energetic. (Applause). The Rev. John Tonle hoped that the second year's work would be even better than the first year, and it would be if every man and woman thoroughly and heartily' entered into the work with the devout intention and purpose to do the Master's will. Noncon- formity had been a long time getting a footing at Winwick but it had got it at last and was going to keep it,'and he believed that in years to come the place would become a centre of large Christian influence and useful- ness. (Applause). The pronouncing of the Benediction brought the pro- ceedings to a close. The collections for the day amounted to £9.

div.head: BOROUGH BUDGET.
div.p: BOROUGH BUDGET.
FOURPENNY REDUCTION OF THE RATES.
Statement at the Council Meeting.

Tuesday was what is known as "Budget night" at the meeting of the Town Council, and the welcome announcement was made that the estimates would allow of a reduction of 4d.in the rates for the coming year. The rates will therefore stand at is. 41. in the £ as against 7s. Sd. during the past year. Alderman FAIRCLOUGIT, as chairman of the Finance Committee, made the Budget statement as follows It is very satisfactory to be able to say that the result on the year's working has been that

A LARGE SUM IS IN RAND on both borough rate and improvement rate accounts. (Hear, hear.) As far as the borough rate is concerned, we close with an estimated balance in hand of £1,492. This is brought about by a general underspending by most of the committees, the greatest saving being, how- ever, by the Finance Committee,' mainly through the amount required for county borough purposes being £550 less than the estimate, a saving of £l7O on salaries account, and of £5OO on interest on amounts spent in excess of sanctions. In the improvement rate account the same results may be noted, almost every committee being underspent, the only exceptions being the weights and measures account, which is only £4O overspent, through providing the new sand blast machine which was not estimated for, and the Finance Com- mittee, which is overspent by £277, on the bank interest on property purchased in anticipation of loans. The committees which have made the largest saving are the

Highway 226 Hospital Lo4gford 420 Markets Nightsoil j 357 Street Improvement Scavenging Some of these amounts are due to increased receipts, as well as reduction in expenditure. The improvement rate closes the year with an estimated balance in hand of £3,490, which, in addition to the foregoing reasons, has been brought about by the handsome contribution from the gas department, which, estimated at £9,000, realized £10,407. With reference to the Budget, it is very gratifying to be able to say that the total sum required is £65,106, as against £68,414 last year a reduc- tion of £3,308. This you will see by the notices of motion which I shall presently move, will enable us to

div.p: REDUCE THE RATES FOR THE YEAR

by the sum of fourpence in the pound. (Load applause.) This is the more gratifying because, as you know, the call upon the borough rate by the Education Committee has been increased by £2,889. I might allude to the estimates of one o* two of the committees. In the Watch Department there has, been included the sum of £932, being the expenditure on the New Police Build- ings which the Local Government Board has not sanctioned. The General Purposes estimate is less by nearly £1,300; last year's requirements for Parlia- mentary expenses of £2,soo,have been reduced to £l,OOO. The estimate of the Finance Committee, apart from the education requirements, is less by £BO9, £5OO having been taken out of the requirements for county borough expenses, and the item of interest on amounts spent in excess of sanction has been reduced to £460. The total requirements ()Mho borough rate are £35,530 4s. 11d., as against £35,493 Is. 11d, last year, an increase only of £B2. The call on the overseers will therefore be practi- cally the same as last year, and they propose to levy a similar poor rate of 4s. 4d. On the improvement rate account, the total requirements are £27,799, as against £30,352 last year, a reduction of £2,553. The only com- mittees I need allude to are the flospital,which is £615 less, and the Markets, which is £4lB less. lam glad to say the hospital has had forsome time very fewpatients, a condition which the Medical Superintendent expects will, in all probability, be likely to continue for some time. In the Markets Department, the Peter-street roof instalment only requires £370 to complete it, as against £5OO in the, estimate of last year, and the painting (£250) is practically finished. The require- ments of the Finance Committee are, however, £1,920 more, through the extra requirements for interest and sinking fund on the new loans sanctioned during the year. We end the year, however, with an estimated balance in hand of £3,490. A rate of 2s. Bd. in the £ will produce a sum of £27,360, and this will be only £419 short of the requirements, and may be covered by the increased rating of certain important new premises in course of construction. ALDERMAN BENNETT AND EFFICIENCY. Alderman BENNETT secopded and said he would like to say how gratifying it !Mist be to all of them to hear the good things which Alderman Fairclough had told them of. and which the members of the Finance Com- mittee had known about for some little time. What the Alderman had stated would be a great relief to many of the ratepayers in the borough, and he trusted the speech would tend to somewhat modify the harsh judgments which had been passed upon this unfortunate Conseil which in face of considerable dilaculties was honestly trying to do its duty. He could assure them that there was no desire to be extravagant. The INIAYOe : What about the Education Committee? Alderman BENNETT : The Education Committee, least of all. There is no desire to be extravagant, and all the committees, with the exceptions which have been named to-night, have noderspent their estimates. Continuiry, the Alderman said the Education Committee was the unfortunate" Aunt Sally "at which they were all so willing to shie these unnecessary missiles. (Laughter). Still it was able to take care of itself,and inthe Corporation would leave it to conduct its own business in its own way it would be more satisfactory than having tkese constant interferences by those who did not always understand what was necessary and did not always look at the matter in its broadest way. The fact that the Education estimates had increased by a considerable figure only emphasised the importance of the news they had heard that night and proved how strong the position of the Council was. It would be folly to lead the Council to hope that they would not have to spend more on education. Of course they would, and he hoped they would spend, in spite of the widespread horror of the high rates, and have a due regard for the necessities of the town. He hoped they would not stultify themselves in their grasping at this ideal of low rates and prove unworthy of the high duties which devolved upon them with regard to the education of the young. (Hear, hear.) He considered that it would be in the best interests of the children, if education were made a national charge, as he was afraid local prejudices and occasionally a narrowness of local view at present tended to jeopardise those interests. He shared in the desire for economy, but it must be coupled with efficiency. There was no real economy if they did not get efficiency. His'one fear was that in the zeal for economy the Council would grasp at the shadow and miss the substance, and the I progressive movement which had been taking place in Warrington of late years might be set back, because of the bogey of the rates. He con- gratulated Alderman Fairclough both as chairman of the Finance Committee and as chairman of the Gas Committee. It was most pleasing to find how in the stress of their financial difficulties the Gas Com- mittee had in the last few years come so nobly to their aid. That fact furnished in his view a conclusive argu- ment against those gentlemen who were constantly endeavouring to belittle what was known as thunicipal I trading in the sense of the municipality undertaking manufacturing concerns. The result they had seen in the case of the gas works would, he thought, ultimately be seen in other departments, and he hoped the trams, electricity works, and waterworks would bring in large sums. He was certain that if they were managed on wise and progressive lines, all these departments would be of the utmost possible advantage to the town. Conncillor Prat nenToN was pleased there was to be a reduction of the rater, but he could not agree with all Alderman Bennett had said. No doubt lase meant right, but unfortunately it was not business. In the Past they had had too much sentiment in the Council, and too little business. There was such a thing as getting efficiency cheaply ; they wanted to get their efficiency as cheaply as it was to be obtained in any , town in England. If they (lid not do so, they would I kill the goose that laid the golden egg. Cheap rates • encouraged more manufacturers to come to the town and induced those who were here to stay. There was no doubt the Education Committee had done good work, , but there had been extravagance in some ways. Councillor MAGI contended that no one realised more the importance of education than those who had experienced the loss of it—(hear, hear)—but he would ' like to know what had the children and the ratepayers I got for the increased expenditure. How many more children were being educated than there were four years ago and bow many more teachers were being employed?' He admired Alderman Bennett as a poet. (Laughter.) 1 He was a fine man, but he had not told them they had
