div.head: Confirmation Service.
div.p: Confirmation Service.

The Bishop of Liverpool conducted a confirmation service at the Parish Church on Saturday afternoon, when 174 candidates were presented-61 from the Parish Church. 10 from the Grammar School, 31 from St. George's Mission, and 72 from St. Clement's Mission. The clergy present were the Revs. Canon Willis, E. J. Willcocks, T. A. J. Ridpath, and T. W. Barber. The Bishop delivered two addresses, in which he asked the candidates never to forget their confirmation and the promises they had made that day. They must fight for the Lord, be faithful unto Him unto their life's end and live as He lived. Mr. Darby presided at the organ.

Wycliffe P.S.A. Society. Mr. Joseph Monks, junr., presided over the meeting of the above on Sunday. There was a fair attendance. The Chairman spoke upon "Duty to Grd and man." He made reference to the very unhappy life of the , multi-millionaire, Mr. Rockefeller. Money got honestly and squarely need not give pain, but could be used to the honour and glory of God.—Mr. Bathgate. of Liver- pool, spoke upon How we are made up—God's great work upon the body, mind and spirit*" God had given to the child its faculties or senses, these wore great gifts. The great universe, the great mind, will and love of God to man and the world, filled us with awe, love and veneration.—Mr. Roberts and the Secretary took part in the meeting.—Mr. Pay- ton, Mits. Bac., presided at the organ.—The Secretary welcomed 8 new members; total now 4.l2—The Secre- tary referred to one of the members, Mr. Irvine, who was shortly leaving to take up his new home in Canada. The Society wished him a happy passage and a pros- perous future.
-Rev. H. Dunnico and Religious Education.

The Rev. H. Dunnico delivered a lecture at Kensing- ton Baptist Church, Liverpool on Wednesday evening, entitled "Free Churchmen and the Education Ques- tion." There was a fair attendance, over whom the Rev. Fred Bennett, of Stockton-on-Tees, presided. In the course of his remarks the Rev. H. Donnie() said the question was one of the greatest importance to the country's future. One of the most distressing features of the English educational system was that the people who ought to be the most concerned were the most apathetic and indifferent. Hitherto the foremost per- sons in the education question were the priest, the parson, and the professional politician. When the parents shook off this apathy they would say to these people, " Get you gone,' and would see that the ques- tion was settled on such wise and liberal lines that every lad and girl would be able to rise step by step, limited only by the child's ability. They repeatedly heard that the Anglican Church had been the first to I show any regard for education, and that but for the Church prior to 1870 there would have been no elemen- tary education at all. He denied that entirely ; the claim of the Anglican Church was insupportable. It was owing to the bishops in the House of Lords that a bill for the establishment of a national system was rejected in 18 ll,four years before the formation of the National, or Church Society.

div.head: Latchford Baptist Church.
div.p: Latchford Baptist Church.

----- -- Preaching on Sunday evening last at the Latchford Baptist Church from Jeremiah Ifith, "As clay in the hands of the potter," the Rev. J. F. Matthews said that in general, prophecy must always be regarded as having an historic setting. It might be difficult to say exactly what were the historical facts, or the social conditions, or the political outlook of any particular prophecy, nevertheles it should be remembered that the utterances of the prophets were always governed by such con- siderations. On the whole perhaps Jeremiahl was less difficult of interpretation in this respect than most of the other prophets. One thing was common to them all. They were eeuer'rned with the declension of Jewish religious life. To Jeremiah Israel's political decadence, and her ruin by the foreign foe,wris directly duo to this cause. He therefore in this passage represented God's sovereign power everted for the destruction as well as the uprearing of a nation under the metaphor of the "Clay in the hands of the potter." God's pro- cesses for fashioning men were often cast in the mould of suffering. It was a serious reflection upon our in- consistency and waywardness that we accepted the sternest discipline for the attairiment of excellence in most walks of life. The lazy grumbled at the intoler- ant burden, the man of sense accepted it for its bene- ficent action in fitting him for his work. Only when the discipline was stern and severe, only when life " Was dipped in baths of hissing tears And battered with the shocks of doom To shape and use." did man arraign the purpose, intelligence, love, and providence of God. If, however, Christ was what we think he claimed to be, if Ile had " tho consciousness of being God's Son in some special sense and degree," nay, if Ho was an adumbration of God Himself, united by the prevailing conditions of age and time and humanity, what was to be said of the passion, the agony of the Cross, and the death on Calvary ? What, if after all the Infinite pity and ineffable love of the Eternal gathered up all the discipline of pain and the mystery of suffer- ing unto Himself in the person of the Saviour ! Was that not a sufficient reason for our eager acceptance of a similar burden, with the treasured sustenance of Divine grace ? Only as we mounted the hilis did the stretch of landscape grow in magnitude. When as from some Pisgah height, we saw life's highway like a stretch of desert through which we had passed, we should see its discipline' like sunlit oases, where ixse bad eaten of the luscious fruit, and imbibed the cooling waters. So should we be thankful that "Through the sorrrow and the strife, The agony and tears, God's hand appears, Moulding our imperfect life And our imperfect years." Medical Missionary Work, Public Meeting in the Parr Hall.

The splendid work which is being done by the Medical Mission Auxiliary of the Church Missionary Society was interestingly explained at a public meeting held in the Parr Hall on Monday evening. There was a good attendance, the Ven. Archdeacon Madden pre- siding. Amongst those present on the platform were : —Dr. S. W. Sutton, M. D. Loud. (medical Missioner of North-West India), Rev. G. J. Howson, M.A. (Rector of St.Mary's,Crumpsall,Manchester and examining chaplin to the Bishop of Livetpool), the Rev. W. R. Cole (secretary of the medital missionary branch for the North West of England), the Revs. James Davies (local hon. secretary), 'W. Bracecamp, G. Vale Owen, H. A. Lester, It. H. Bowen, T. A. J. Ridpath, and H. R. Wild. A united choir drawn from the local churches was in attendance and led the singing of the hymns. Mr. E Wilkes, A.L.C.M., presided at the organ. The ARCIIDSACON, said that last year, at this annual meeting, thoy had a visit from Dr. Cook. He (the

Chairman) was one of the speakers, and he should never forget the address which the doctor delivered. It was the most thrilling, the most telling, and at the same time a revelation of the self-sacrifice of their men in the mission field. When they remembered what he told them about the sleeping sickness and of the many victims to that terrible disease he was sure they would all be thankful to know that he was at work again in Mango, and that he had been presented with a dispensary with all the expenses paid, even the medicine to some extent, for six months. There he was doing a wonder- ful work in the capital of Uganda. (Applause.) It was a good thing to have the missionaries at home for a little holiday and rest, and it gave Englishmen an opportunity of seeing them. The great medical mission- ary work was growing in popularity all over the country, and they had only to read of the suffering of some of the people of India and Africa, and the tortures they went through, at the hands of their own medicine men, to appreciate from the human point of view the great and noble work that was being done. Of course it was not merely the healing of the body they aimed at ; they followed the example of Him who not only said : "Rise, take up thy bed and walk," but also, "Son, thy sins are forgiven thee, go in peace " ; so that behind the work of the medical missionary there stood the figure of the blessed Master who while He healed the body also spoke words of healing to the soul. (Applause.) Dr. SUTTON gave a highly interesting description of medical missionary work at Quetta, 100 miles from Kandahar, to which station he was sent twenty-one years ago. He alluded to the difficulties experienced by the missionaries,pointing that there were three different native races, each with a language of its own, and the people were most bigoted and fanatical Mohammedans. Dr. Sutton showed hoW by tending the sick he was able to gain opportunities of preaching the Gospel which otherwise would doubtless have been denied hirn. God had blessed and prospered the work at Quetta, that they now hada flourishing medical mission. There was a large hospital and a bungalow for the workers, and branch dispensaries were now to be provided at the request of the native ruler in neighbouring places. A Church had also been built for the native Christians. Dr. Sutton described the work in the hospital, pointing that while patients were in the waiting room portions of scripture were expounded to them. When people became in- patients they received consecutive Christian teaclling. They in England could have no idea of how far-reaching the influence of a place like that was. He instanced how people had travelled several hundred miles to receive treatment at the hospital and through the efforts of the workers many natives had been converted to Christianity. (Applause). The Rev. G. J. HowsoN said that if there was one cause that was very close to the heart of the Bishop of the diocese it was the extension of God's Kingdom in foreign lands. He was sure the Bishop would wish his ordination candidates if not to pass an examination in the knowledge of foreign missions, at any rate to be very deeply interested in the work of God in foreign lands. God had allowed medical missions to prosper first qf all because they had been undertaken in obedi- ence to the command of the Lord. It was extra- ordinary to think that it was only in modern times that the appreciation of our Lord's laying down these lines of work had been realized. Having found out a clue to the obedience of the bidding of the Master those missions were prospering. The second reason for their success was because there , had been a distinct use of the prayer for the wisdom given by the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit had guided those marvellous tactfulnesses those wonderful adapta- tions to circumstances of which they had heard that night. Then again, men had seen that love was at the back of the preaching of the Gospel, and there had also been an extraordinary development of the power of endurance and courage. It was the duty of Christians in England to think over what God had done for them and to realize all He had revealed to them, and then they would wish to share xshat they possessed. The clergy must be careful that they had their ideal up high in regard to foreign missionary work, for water most find its own level and if the clergy did not take an interest in foreign missions their people would not. The speaker concluded by urging his hearers to read more about missions,to support them, and to pray for their success. A short address was also delivered by the Rev. W. R. Cole and the meeting closed with the Benediction.

div.head: Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church.
div.p: Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church.

At this Church on Sunday morning the Rev. Sidney Pitt preached on "The problem of pain," his text being Psalm 73. verses 10 and 11. Hs pointed out amongst other things that pain might be regarded as a back- ground to pleasure. That was the doctrine of Dr. Punshon's hYmn " Sweet is the sunlight after rain, and sweet the sleep that follows pain." Those who felt it would, he was sure, appreciate it. When at last the tooth was out or the racking limb hadceasA to torment, what a luxury it was to throw oneself down at ease, or after sleepless,tossing hours,to lay one's head upon the pillow with the prospect of a night of sleep. It was not merely that one could appreciate ease better after suffering, but there was in reality an added sweetness in it—a reaction, a penetrating comfort which did to a certain extent make up for what one had lost. The pro- portion of suffering to ease in human life was after all a small one. Except in someextraordinary case,we had a score of days of health and pleasure for one of pain. Most of us had a hundred, many a thousand, and if these occasional experiences of pain added a zest and appreci- ation to the rest, there was to that extent an explana- tion of them. What would a picture be if it were all light ? It was on the distribution of shades that the effect depended. Or What use would an oratorio be if it were all smooth and sweet? The great masters did not leave their work like that. They put the rolling thunders and the harsh discords here and there. What would a sunset be if it were nothing but a red fire ball sinking out of sight every day? It was when the clouds gathered round that we saw the golden glories which constituted the noblest sight on earth. Considerations like those had led Adelaide Ann Proctor to say : "I thank Thee more that all our jO3 is touched with pain, That shadows fall on brightest hours That thorns remain So that earth's bliss may. be our guide And not our chain." At the evening service Mr. John Upson preached on the words : "Thou 0 Father hat been the guide of my youth."

div.head: Church Society Addresses.
div.p: Church Society Addresses.

The Rev. J. H. Thorpe, of Stockport, who had been announced to speak on Duty "at last Friday evening's service for men at the Parish Church was unable to fulfil the engagement, but an excellent substitute Wag found in the Rev. C. C. Elcum, Vicar -of S. Agnes' Church, Liverpool. There was again a large attendance and the address, which was of a practical, helpful character, was listened to with deep attention. The rev. gentleman took for his text the words : " Whatsoever ye do, do it heartily as to the Lord and not unto men." Our Christian duty, he said, might be divided under three heads—we had to fight, work, and suffer. The preacher dealt chiefly with the duty of work. God, he said, wished everyone to work and there was really no room for idlers in the Church of Christ. No one who had been idle in a wrong sense in this world, he made bold to say, would find himself at home in Heaven. Did they think that [leaven was only a place for singing hymns and being idle in a holy way? Sorely not. If they were to pray that God's will might be done ,in this world in the same way that it was done in Eleaven,they must mean that in this world they had to apprentice themselves for the life of good work above. In this world a large amount of what they were doing would be so much litter that would have to be swept away when the great work of Heaven began. Yet they felt that God had put them in this world in their various callings and that God Himself had laid upon them the duty of work which they had got to do. The truest Christian would be the best workman and would prove by the good quality of his work that he was a genuine Christian. the preacher urged his hearers not to be ashamed of their work, however humble, if it was done in the spirit of an offering to God. They must not be carried away by the snobbish thoughts of now-a-days that one par- ticular kind of work was more worthy than another. Every bit of true work was capable of being built into the great altar of self-sacrifice to God. This (Friday) evening the concluding address of the series will be delivered by the-Rev. Paul Bull, of the Community of the Resurrection, whose subject will be " Social purity." The rev, gentleman, says the "Man- chester Guardian," has been described as " the fibers of the Anglican pulpit." No doubt there is a good deal of painful realism in his teachings and writings, but it represents at most only a superficial phase of his work, and is generally nothing more than a means to an end. Probably no preacher of to-day appeals so directly and so widely to the hearts of Churchmen. His recent courageous utterances on social problems and his pointed denunciation of luxury among the rich and leisured classes may almost be said to have created a new current of thought in the Anglican Church. llis recent articles in the " Church Times " on "Redeeming the time " have had quite a staggering effect on the complacent, well-to-do, and severely individualist Churchman. Some- what like a piercing wind, they find the weak points in the pampered or unsound constitution, but act only as a tonic upon the really robust.

div.head: SALE OF WORK AT BEWSEY-ROAD.
div.p: SALE OF WORK AT BEWSEY-ROAD.
Succeessful Effort on Behalf of the Trust Funds.

The congregation of Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church have this week been engaged in an effort, by means of their annual sale of work, to reduce the debt on the trust 'funds of the Church, and the event has proved highly successful. The sale was opened in the Lecture Hall adjoining the Church on Wednesday afternoon by Mr. J. Taylor, L.D.S., and was continued on Thurs- day. Thanks to the willing help of the ladies, there was a splendid display of useful and fancy wares and the room, which has recently been re-decorated, presented a bright and pleasing appearance. The following ladies presided at the stalls :—Flower stall : Mrs. and Miss Hayward, Miss Dora Roberts. Tea room : Mesdames Mitchell, Williams, A. Parkinson and Sinclair, and Miss Pitt. Refreshment stall : Mrs. and Miss Taylor, Mrs. T Winstanley, Mrs. Hipkiss. Fancy stall : Mesdames Savage, Joseph Bsiley, C. Healey and Bailey. Work stall : Mesdames W. Winstanley, Pitt, Upson, Walker, Rowland and Corbett, and Miss Healey. Young Ladies' Work stall : Misses Bailey, Dora Pitt, Upson, M. Thomas and Mason.

Alderman Tinnion presided at Wednesday's opening ceremony, and the attendance included Mr. John Taylor (who opened the sale), the Revs. S. Pitt, W. Mellor, and J. Manning ; Mr. J. W. Hayward and Mr. J. Upson.—The Chairman said the fact of Mr. Taylor's coming to open \ the sale was only one link in a long chain of kindnesses which he had rendered to Methodism and Bewsey-road Church. He had helped the Circuit splendidly in rdany ways, and not least in the capacity of circuit steward. He (Alderman Tinnion) had always had a very warm interest in Bewsey-road. He joined as a member many years ago and he admired the work which was being done by the Church in the midst of an artisan and working class community. It was a very commendable trait in the character of the congregation that the members were determined if they possibly could to carry on the work free from clebt,but as the ordinary sources of income were not sufficient to meet the expenditure the annual sale had to be resorted to. He trusted the effort would be a great success. (Applause.) Mr. TAYLOR., after congratulating the chairman on the well-deserved honour bestowed upon him by the Council in electing him to an aldermanic seat, said they ought all to love their Church. He believed the Wes- leyan Church was among the foremost in all active Christian work and it had taken the lead in the build- ing of huge mission halls which had been a great bless- ing in reaching the masses in many of the large towns. Perhaps the weakest link in the chain of Methodism was the teaching in the Sunday schools. Teachers were accepted without any preparation or examination and the result was that many were unfit for the work they had undertaken. He hoped the day would not be far distant when they would have some system of testing thefltness of teachers before accepting them for work in the Sunday schools. He had been associated with Bewsey-road Church since its opening about thirty-one years ago and had always felt a kind of sacred regard for it. After thanking the lady workers for their valuable help, Mr. Taylor asked all present to do their utmost for the success of the sale. The Rev. S. PITT briefly explained the need for the sale, and said he hoped the time would come when it would be possible to make an effort to extinguish the debt on the trust funds. There was, he said, a very fine element of yorng people at Bewsey road, and Silver-street Sunday School had con- tributed nobly in that direction. He could bear testi- mony to the profound and far-reaching spiritual influence exercised by the work there. He hoped that eventually they would be able to erect more ample premises at Bewsey-road so that their Sunday School might be con- ducted nearer the centre of their operations. On the motion of the Rev. W. Msmort seconded by Mr. J. W. Hayward, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the Chairman and to Mr. Taylor and the business of the sale commenced. THURSDAY'S PROCEEDINGS.

The opening ceremony on Thursday was performed by Miss Dodds, Penketh, in the presence of a large attendance, over which Miss Mary Dodds presided. The Rev. S. Prrr announced that the proceedings thn previous day realized £52, a result which they con- sidered highly satisfactory. (Applause.) He heartily welcomed the ladies who had come to preside and to open the sale, and whom he thought were that day making their entrance upon public life of that kind. They could not make a beginning at a more appropriate place than Bewsey-road on account of the old association of Mr. and Mrs. Dodds with that II Church (Applause.) Missa:Martv DODDS expressed her pleasure at being present and at being able to help, in a small way, the friends at Bewsey-road. She heard with pleasure of the splendid result of the previous day's sale and hoped that the proceedings that day would be equally success- ful and that they would realize even more than the amount which they desired to raise. (Applause.) Miss DODDS said that although she was not accustomed to occupying such a position she felt that it was quite impossible to refuse the request of such an old friend as Mr. Upson. She was very pleased to be present and to assist such a worthy object as that for which the sale was being held. She hoped the pro- ceedings would be very successful and had much , pleasure in declaring the bazaar open. (Applause.) Miss BESSIE, DUTTON moved a vote of thanks to the Misses Dodds for their services. Some very sarcastic remarks were made about " platform ladies" and covert sneers were thrown at them. She agreed that it was a splendid thing for ladies to work in private but at the same time she thought they could have a very great influence in a public way. (Hear, hear.) The ladies of Warrington had touched one or two public things and while they certainly could do good work privately, public work, she thought would not injure them in the least. (Hear, hear.) Miss Mary Dodds had taken a very useful and honourable part as secretary of a temperance organization in the town and her sister had done equally useful work. (Applause.) Mr. UPSON seconded the vote of thanks,and on behalf of himself and the• workers expressed his indebtedness to the two ladies for their services. At Bewsey-rohd they wanted to get rid of the incubus of debt which was pressing upontliem,limiting their efforts and taking away from them some of the energy which would other- wise be devoted to agressive work. (Applause.) The vote was heartily accorded, Miss Mary Dodds briefly responding. Mrs. DODDS, who rose in response to a request from'.- Mr. Pitt, said she was always pleased to visit Bewsey- road as it was the first Wesleyan church she attended when she came to Warrington, and as many happy memories were associated with the church. She hoped they would be able to clear elf the debt. They had succeeded in doing so at Penketh in regard to the Sunday School and felt much lighter and brighter, and she hoped they would be able to do the same at Bewsey- road and that they would be able to seek fresh fields and pastures new without anything to hinder them. (Applause.) Mr. JAMES DODDS also briefly responded to a request that he should speak. The business of the sale then commenced. The total proceeds of the sale amounted to the handsome sum of £lOO.

div.head: DRAMATIC SOCIETY'S COMPLAINT.
div.p: DRAMATIC SOCIETY'S COMPLAINT.

THE SMOKE NUISANCE. Can it be Abated P One of the principal questions to which the Beauti- ful Warrington Society is addressing itself is the abate- ment of the smoke nuisance and an jute, esting lecture on" Smoke prevention "was delivered in the Co-opera - tive Hall, on Thursday evening by Mr. J.B.C. Kershaw, F.I.C. The meeting, which was largely attended, was presided over by Councillor Fulton Smith. The lecturer after dealing with the general aspects of the question gave some useful hints in regard to the abatement of smoke from domestic fires which, he pointed out, were responsible for 50 per cent, of the smoke in a town. He suggested that Town Councils should pass bye- laws that grates of a certain pattern constructed on scientific principles should be introduced in all new houses and instanced several ways in which the tenants could help to solve the smoke question. With regard to factories, the lecturer said that in his opinion and in the view of others qualified to judge, smoke was a sign of imperfect combustion and therefore of bad management in the use of coal for heating or steam- raising purposes. He believed that coal of bituminous quality was capable of perfect combustion, and black smoke was so much evidence of improper design or use. That defect might be due either to insufficient know- ledge of scientific principles of combustion on the part of the designer of a furnace or boiler,or to parsimony on the part of the buyer or owner of the plant. The former evil might be removed by education and the latter could only be overcome by a greater insistence that the health and welfare of the general public were of paramount importance and should not be sacrificed to alight pecuniary gains on the side of the smoke pro- ducer. An important point was that at many works the boiler power needed increasing. He believed that in time smoke prevention would become general and that the day would arrive wi,en Warrington would again be that beautiful town the advent of which that Society had been formed to promote and hasten. (Applause.) An interesting discussion followed, Alderman Bennett describing the smoke nuisance as one of the curses af medern civilization and alluding to his unsuccessful efforts to induce the Town Council to deal with offending manufacterers. He pointed out that owing to improved methods of stoking at the electricity works there was a saving to the ratepayers of about £6OO a year and the chimneys did not emit black smoke. Mr. EDWIN' Woos was unconvinced that smoke could be prevented but said he was quite willing to learn. He had been told a certain works in Warrington was saving 1,000 tons of fuel per week but until that was proved to him he would not believe it. Mr. H. KINGDON said the statement which had been made and could be substantiated was that if Messrs. Crosfleld had in operation at Bank Quay the same methods as were in vogue fifteen years ago they would beiburning 1,000 tons more of fuel per week. Of course that was not entirely attributable to smoke prevention. The discussion was also taken part in by Dr. Ormandy (who said the prevention of smoke was almost invari- ably accompanied by economy which in itself more than justified the work that was necessary to produce the desired end), Alderman Stnethumt, Mr. G. Dale and Mr. Allen.
The lecturer was thanked on the proposition of Canon MORLEY STEVENSON, seconded by Mr. L. GREENING.

div.head: Charges for the Use of Parr Hall.
div.p: The Charges for the Use of Parr Hall.

A question arising out of the recent performances by the St. Mary's Dramatic Society came before the Town Council at Tuesday evening's meeting. When the minutes of the Town Hall, Parks and Baths Committee were being considered, Councillor Maginn said he had received a letter from the St. Mery's Dramatic Society with reference to the charge for the use of Parr Hall for the recent performances. He thought the com- munication might have been sent to him earlier but nevertheless he considered the Society's grievance was a genuine one. The MAYOR said the question was out of order as it did not effectithe Town Hall, Parks, and Baths Com- mittee. The committee which had charge of Parr Hall was a sub-committee of the General Purposes Committee. Councillor MAGE,R4 protested that he was entitled to brill., the matter up but amidst loud cries of " chair " I he resumed his seat. Later he referred to the subject when the General Purposes Committee's minutes were ' brought forward. He said the performances of the St. 1 Mary's Dramatic Society were for the benefit of a charity and not for any individual profit, and therefore he thought the complaint deserved attention. Con- tinuing, he said if there was ever a miserable place Parr Hall was that place. It was not heated properly nor lighted properly. The St. Mary's Dramatic Society— and he was not bringing this matter forward because he happened to be a Catholic—were charged £22 Ills. Gd. for the week. He suggested that, as Parr Hall wis I given for the benefit of the public, when anything was being done solely to raise money for the public good some special arrangement might be made. The DEPUTY TOWN CLERK said the charge of £22 I 19s. (Id. was a special one in consideration of the per- formances being for charitable purposes, and the terms were submitted to the Society before-hand. The MAYOR: I think the charge is reasonable. Councillor MAGIEN, again complaining of the condi- tions at the hall remarked. " I have no right to catch cold there, and I am- entitled to every attention. The place is a bear garden." The MAYOR: Do you mean the Parr Hall or the Town Council ? Councillor MAGINY, in conclusion, said things would be different if it was a private hall or a hotel room, and he did not see why Parr Hall should not be properly lighted and heated. The DEpI7TY Tows CLERK Said a letter had been received from the Dramatic Society that day and it would be considered at the next meeting of the Parr ' Hall Committee. On this understanding the matter was allowed to I drop.

div.head: WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT BOWLING LEAGUE.
div.p: WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT BOWLING LEAGUE.

Annual Meeting. The annual meeting of the Warrington and District Bowling League was held at the Bull's Head Inn, Church-street on Thursday evening and was well attended. All the local affiliated clubs were represented and in addition delegates were present from the Norton Arms, Halton, Egerton Arms, Runcorn, Earlestown Bowling Club and the Cuerdley Cross Club.

ELECTION OR OFFICERS. Mr. A. H. Crosileld, M.P., was unanimously re-elected president of the League and the vice-presidents were re-elected as follows : Messrs. J. Allison J. Berry, J. Earle, J. Forster, J. W. Kay, J. Newton, C. E. Parker, J. Roberts, J. Rushworth, W. J. Shaw, S. Taylor, W. Unsworth, J. E. Warren, Alderman Evans and Councillor Wilkinson. Mr. E. Taylor was re-elected hon. secretary, and Mr. G. F. Freeman was again appointed as hon. treasurer. ALTERATION IN THE COMPETITION. The most important business before the meeting a proposal to extend the radius of the League to miles outside the borough boundary and to work - competition this yearon the "knock out" principle. Thed suggestion was heartily and unanimously approved ilø the delegates present from the outside clubs announce,' the intention of the organizations which they repre" seated seeking membership. A number of other clubs, local and others, have been approached and it is con- fidently expected that the majority of these will join the new League. A GLASGOW MOTHER AND HER CHILDREN. VERO'S LIGHTNING COUGH CURE. CURED HER WHOLE FAMILY. Mrs. BUCHANAN, 89, Raeborry Street, Glasgow. writes, October 20th,1901 :—" I think it my duty to give you my opinion of VENO'S LIGHTNING Couox CURE. You could not have given it a better name ; it has proved a Lightning Cough Cure to my four childr3n with whooping cough ; they suffered since last April ; they were all cured in one week by your Cough Cure. X will never be without it. I have given it to most of myk friends because I have so much faith in it. I thought I was going to lose two of my children; they could neither eat nor sleep, but now they can go out in all weathers ; they like your Cough Cure, and won't g 0 to bed without it."
As for VENO S LIGHTNING COUGH CURE at Chemists, 91d., is. id., and 2s. 9d.

NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN in accordance with the provisions of Section 8 (1) of the Education Act. 1902, that the County Council ot the County Palatine of Lancaster, being the Local Education Authority for the purposes of 4,art HI. of that Act, propose to provide a new Public Elementary Sehool for about 12) children at Bitten In the County Palatine of Lancaster. The School will be available for the following area TOWNSHIP OP DITTON. HARCOURT B. CURB, Clerk of the County Council. Dated 7th March, 1908. Section 8(1) of the Education Act,l9o2,providel as follows: •• (I) rbere the Local Education Authority or any other persons propose to nrovide a new public elementary school, they shall give public notice of their intention to ao so, and the Managers of any existing school, or the Local Education Authority (where they are not themselves the persons proposing to provide the school), or any ten ratepayers in the area for which it is proposed to pro- vide the school, may, within three months after the notice is given, appeal to the Hoard of Education on the ground that the proposed school is not required. or that a school provided by the Local Education Authority, or not so provided, as the Case may be, is better suited to meet the wants of the district than the school proposed to be provided, and any school built in contravention of the decision of the Hoard of Education on such appeal shall be treated as unnecessary."

That applied to police as well as officials in Liverpool. COnncillor LORD agreed with that suggestion and, said he would agree to the withdrawal of the resolution on the understanding that itshould be amended in that drastic form. Alderman SMETITURSTgaid his object was that the tramways manager and Matthias and Mr. Purse should travel free. Whether they were on duty or not they would have to look after anything that happened on the cars. If he wa4 the tramways engineer and had to pay his fare when going to dinner and anything happened. he would let it wait until he finished his dinner hour. Conncillor PEIIBEitTON : Oh; you would get the sack. (Laughter). On a vote being taken the amendment was defeated and the-original resolution. carried. THE WATERWO'RRS INQUIRY. Councillor STOTT asked if the Mayor could give any information as to the inquiry into the waterworkscontract and the report presented by Mr. Garside. The Mayon : We are waiting for .4r. Deis' report. The committee have the matter in hand. Councillor STOTT : It is a long time. (Rear, hear.) The Maxon : You cannot force this kind of-thing. The DEenTY TowN CLERK said the. committee expected to have a meeting in the next ten days.

• ST HELENS. _— BETTING RAID AT ST. HELENS. A raid by the St. Helens police in the neighbourhood of Smithy-brow on Tuesday resulted in three women and two men being arrested on charges of betting. The accused are James and John Hollows, of 44, Parr-street, and Ann Mercer, Susan Elliott, and Esther Leahey, all of Parr-street. They were brought before a magistrate and formally remanded for a week. DEATH OF A ST. HELENS WESLEYAN MINISTER. The Rev. Thomas Hollis, of Cowley Hill-lane, St. Helens, superintendent minister of the St. Helens and Prescot Wesleyan Circuit, died on Saturday. Mr. Hollis had been seriously ill for over a week from an internal complaint, and his condition during the last day or two became critical. The deceased gentleman was a fine, stalwart man and a good organiser and preacher. His somewhat untimely death is very much regretted.—Mr. Hollis was fifty-four years of age, and a native of Nottingham. He had been at St. Helens a year and a half, and was previously superintendent minister at Chester. Ile entered the ministry in 1374, and was married, and leaves a widow. He had been actively connected with the schemes for the building of the new churches at Ashton and Burtonwood. The Ashton Church has been built, and the foundation stone of the 13urtonwood edifice was to have been laid this week. BAND OF HOPE WORK AT ST. HELENS. The first great united meeting of the bands of hope connected with the St. Helens Temperence Union was held at the Town Hall on Monday, and proved of excep- tional interest to 311 concerned. The Rev. Cyril , Bardsley, vicar, presided, being supported by the Revs. ' W. A. Eyre (Primitive Methodist), and W. H. Perkins (Wesleyan), Mr. J. B. Leach, and a large number of local ministers and temperance workers. Recitation and singing competitions wereadjudicated on by Messrs. , W. G. Newnes, A.L.C.111., and S. J. Newnes, and there was a large distribution of prizes. During the winter I temperance lessons have been given at. the various bands of hope meetings, and a competition took place for the champion banner. St. Mary's Mission Parish Church, Nut-grove Wesley, and Ravenhead, St. John's Bands of Hope competed. St. Mary's and the Parish Church headed the contest, four members of each gaining the maximum marks. St. Mary's had seven competitors who gained the maximum, and so the banner was awarded to and will be held by St. Mary's for the first year. Twenty-four first prizes were won by the children from the four schools above, and these were provided, in the shape of handsome books, by Sir David Gamble Bart., who signed each book. The secretaries, Messrs. W. J. B. Dixon and W. S. Else, carried out the arrangements most efficiently. RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS. County Council Expenditure. The fortaightly meeting of the Runcorn 13)ard of Guardians was held at Dutton on Tuesday when there were present :—Messrs. A. R. Norman (presiding), C. Roylance, J. Bolshrtw, A. H. Talbot, A. Broom, T. Baxter, C. E. Linaker, J. H. Davies, J. Smith, T. Wright, T. Guest, S. Woodward, W. Harrison, G. Pilling, J. Spruce, W. M. Morris, P. Collins, J. W. Temperley, Hallows, J. Whitley, R. Billington, C. E. Linaker, Jun., A. G. Guest, T. Antwis, G. F. Ashton (clerk), W. E. Hough (assistant clerk), Cook, Pearson and de Prez (relieving officers), and J. Cunnah (workhouse master). VACCINATION. The Leigh Union forwarded the following resolution "That in the opinion of this Board, a conferehce of representatives from every union in England and Wales should be convened to discuss the financial side of the vaccination question, and that at such conference a deputation be appointed to wait upon the president of the Local Government Board, for the purpose of urging upon him the immediate necessity of some amendment of the vaccination acts and the order of the Local Government Board made thereon." Mr. C. E. Linaker thought they all objected to the high charges for vaccination and also to the principal upon which vaccination as conducted. (Hear, bee). It was unanimously decided to send delegates to the conference. COUNTY EXPENDITURE. The Bucklow Union forwarded the following resolu- tion for approval: "That this Board views with alarm the steady increase in the amount of the County rate for education and invites co-operation of other Boards of Guardians in making a formal protest against the increase." (Applause) It was decided unanimously to support the Bucklow Union. <SP RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL. _ Crossley Sanatorium. The fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Rural Dis- I trict Council was held at Dutton on Tuesday when I there were present :—Messrs. S. Woodward (presiding), ' C. Roylance, J. Bolshaw, A. H. Talbot, A. Broom, T. Baxter, C. E. Linaker, J. H. Davies, J. Smith, T. Wright, T. Guest, W. Harrison, G. Pilling, J. Spruce, J. Hallows, J. Whitley, R. Billington' C. E. Linaker, jun. ' A. G. Guest, T. Antwis, G. F. Ashton, (clerk), W. E. Hough (assistant clerk), W. Diggle, and J. , Swinton (surveyors) and J. Farrington (inspector) ' I Mr. Morris asked for information as to the settle- ment of the question of the assessment of the Crossley Sanatorium. I A lengthy discussion ensued as to the advisability of making the result public. Mr. Linaker pointed out that the Assessment Com- mittee was supposed to adjust the assessment on fair and equitable lines and they did so. To decline to I make the figures public made it appear as though there was something to he ashamed of. Upon a vote being taken it was decided to publish the agreed assessment which the Clerk announced as £760 gross £665 rateable. TREE PLANTING. Mr. Linaker asked if there was to be a report from any committee with reference to Stockton Heath. If there was he had something to say. Mr. Woodward : I can assure you that I will allow no discussion on that subject to-day. SURVEYORS' SALARIES. Dr. Diggle applied for an increase in salary. He pointed out that 17 miles of roads had been added to i his district and remunerative work had been taken away from him whilst his salary had not been altered. It was decided to leave the question to the Highways Executive Committee who were instructed to consider the question of Swinton's salary at the same time it being intimated that Mr. Swinton also desired an advance. PENKETH. I LECTIIRE BY MR. H. CONGREVE.—There was a large I gathering in Penkoth Wesleyan school on Monday evening when Mr. Hubert Congreve, of Moore, gave his splendid illustrated lecture entitled " A tour through the Highlands of Southern Franco." For nearly two hours the lecturer held his audience enthralled with the interesting description he gave of this little known but uncommonly beautiful district. The slides were very numerous and pictured the country and its people in a way which did credit to Mr. Congreve's skill and taste as a photographer. At the close a very hearty vote of thanks was accorded the lecturer, and to Mrs. Dodds for her services in the chair.

Ode at Chemists everywhere. • • " OBSERVER " CUP FINAL. • Oughtrington Park Victorious. The final for the local Association Cup drew a large crowd to the Walker's Brewery ground on Saturday. Oughtrington started before a record attendance, and the Park men early setting up a fine pace, the general run of the game was located in the Northwich Victoria ' quarters. Rose early on dealt with a movement , initiated by Mather and Leigh. Clever passing by Dula and Hughes was checked by L. Thomason, but North- wich would not be denied, and Dale tested Ilobin from long range. The attack was maintained by the " Salttnen," and after Bobin had Save from Hodgkin- son, Dale again caused trouble, and Hobin failing to clear Hodgkinson sent the bell into the net. Oughtrington immediately got down and dropping shots by Mather and .1. Leah were turned over the bar by Stubbs. Near the interval Thomason gave away a couple of penalties, but Gandy and Dale failed signally to turn them to good account, and at half-time North- wich , led by one goal to nil. Turning round, Oughirington made the pace and after Stubbs had saved repeatedly, Mather put on the _finishing touch to a corner. Oughtrington continued 711. show capital form. L. Thomason served his forwards well, and J. Leah and H. Leigh making a fine run on the right, Mather scored by heading the ball into the net after Stubbs had failed to clear. Thik proved the winning point of the match, and Oughtrington deservedly won by two. goals to one. Teams :—Oughtrington Park: Goal, J. Robin; full backs, F. Thomason and G. Short; half backs, F. Lord, L. Thomason and T. Marley; forwards' A. Lord, H. Thomason (captain), J. Leah, H. Leigh and G. Mather. Northwich Victoria: Goal, C. Stubbs ; full backs, J. A. Rose and Win. Harts; half back ; L. Isherwood, H. Gandy and J. Bracegirdle ; forwards, A. Lees, H. Johnson. M. Dale, W. H. Hughes and J. Hodgkinson. The cup was afterwards presented to the winning teem by the President of the Associa- tion, Councillor Fulton Smith. COMMITTEE ENTERTAINED. 1 I Later in the evening the committee and officers of the Association were entertained to dinner at the' Lion Hotel. An excellent repast was served by Mr. John Lee and the proceedings were of a most enjoyable character. Quarternmsrer-sergeant J. P. Hallins pre- side(' and upon his proposition the usual toasts were honoured. The Chairman also submitted" The Presi- dent and Vice-Presidents "—a toast which was received with musical honour?. Councillor FULTON-SMITH responded. He was very pleased that Association football was making itself really felt in Warrington, which, he thought, was owing in a very large measure to the efforts-of the Executive Committee of the Association. There was still the same enthusiasm for the Rugby -code, but if they could only have Association exemplified as it had been that after- noon they would have much larger support. (Hear, hear.) He was rather amused to have been congratu- lated by the Chairman upon being a member of the town Council. The position was not an honorary one, but was one to which there was a great deal of work of which the general public knew nothing. At the next meeting of the Council there wmild be a very fair and creditable balance sheet to be submitted In spite of the outcry, regarding expenditure, rased by a certain section who glorified themselves by stating that they were the only true representatives of the rate- payers. The real work was done at the committee meetings where they had many hours of really hard thinking but, some of the meetings were such that they were, to him, actually a form of recreation—meetings of which matters were discussed quietly and dispassion- ately, and at which though they had their differences they were courteous towards each otherand worked for the best interests of the town. (Applause.) Mr. J. Le:wis (Bootle) submitted the toast oi " The Association." As the first chairman of the Association he spoke of the bard struggle which they had in the earlier years to maintain their existence. Ho briefly touched upon the experiment of running a professional Association team in I‘arrington—an experiment which proved to be a failure. Warrington, however, was large enough to support two teams, nod before long they would have to run a professional Association team. During his speechalr. Lewis highly praised the work of Mr. T. P. Bradthaw, boa. secietary of the Assoc!ation (Applause). The toast, with which Mr. Bradshaw's name was coupled, was received with musical honours. 'Mr. BRADSHAW and the CHAIRMAN both briefly res- ponded.a On the proposition of Mr. W. H. SMALLEY, the toast of "rhe Observer Co." was drunk, Mr. K DRAPER and Mr. H. ISHKRWOOD responding. During the evening on excellent musical programme was submitted. Songs were given by Mr. T. Humphseys, Mr. J. Draper, Colour-Sergeant Kelly and Mr. W. Deradet t ; whistling solos being effectively given by Drummer Cleeson. Mr. 'l'. Taylor acted aa accom- papist.
